subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT APPOINTMENT PROCESS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today is an historic day in the judicial history of Canada marked by the swearing in of Madam Justice Bertha Wilson as a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. The appointment of this respected and accomplished jurist has been applauded by Canadians from coast to coast.
The appointment of the first woman to the Supreme Court of Canada was a result, in part, of strong representations by the official opposition and by widespread public input. In view of the imminent patriation of the Canadian Constitution, including the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which will substantially increase the role and power of the Supreme Court of Canada in the determination of the rights and liberties of Canadian citizens, it is incumbent upon legislators to reassess the process of appointment to the Supreme Court of Canada, now the sole prerogative of the Prime Minister. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer):
That this House direct an immediate reference to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on the process of judicial appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada, including the involvement of the House of Commons in the review and confirmation of nominees to the Supreme Court of Canada.

CALL FOR REMOVAL OF EXCISE TAX ON NATURAL GAS AND HOME HEATING OIL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to take exception to a reply given by the Prime Minister during question period yesterday. He said the way to bring down interest rates and thereby stimulate our economy is to "bring down inflation, to bring down costs", etc. Yet he says one thing and does another. His government has been the most profligate spender in our history and is doing literally nothing to check spending and cut outlays. He demonstrates daily that the situation is clearly beyond him, and he has no quotations from Chairman Mao to bail him out.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That, if he is to be credible, the Prime Minister should practice what he preaches. Bring down costs-as he says-and a good starting point would be the removal of the nearly 30 per cent excise tax on natural gas and oil for home heating purposes, thereby cutting home owners' heating costs by almost one third.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TAX MEASURES ON CAR RENTAL BUSINESSES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, an all too often forgotten victim of the November 12 budget is the automobile dealer who is trying to sell cars at exorbitant interest rates and trying to operate a leasing business. Over 2,500 dealers, leasing upwards of 800,000 automobiles, will lose a full 15 per cent of their depreciation allowance on the cost of new cars due to the budget's halving of the capital cost allowance. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That, as this tax measure is expected to result in a surge of auto dealer bankruptcies and closures, the Minister of Finance should heed the warning signs and withdraw the proposal before it is too late to rescue 2,500 dealers.

subtopic: CONTRACT FOR SALE OF GENERAL MOTORS CARS TO IRAQ
CONTRACT FOR SALE OF GENERAL MOTORS CARS TO IRAQ
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to put a question to the Minister of State for International Trade with respect to the deal between General Motors and Iraq for the sale of cars. Has General Motors received formal notification from Iraq that it is not its intention to accept delivery and pay for the cars which are sitting on the Halifax docks?

March 30, 1982
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subtopic: CONTRACT FOR SALE OF GENERAL MOTORS CARS TO IRAQ
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot honestly say whether General Motors has received formal notice. I have been told by the Iraqi ambassador, who has just returned from Baghdad, that the deal will not be consummated.
Madam Speaker, can the minister tell us why the deal will not be consummated with the Iraqis? What are the grounds for cancelling or withdrawing from the contract?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, I do not think the Iraqi authorities acknowledge that there is a contract for the second fleet of cars. I am informed that this particular contract was still being negotiated. The reason given to me by the Iraqi authorities for not exercising the option on the second lot of 12,500 cars was the fact that they felt the mechanical problems with the first
13,000	cars were such that they did not want to take the second order.

Madam Speaker, I am informed by General Motors that they do have a contract which they consider binding. I would have thought the minister might know whether or not a contract exists. But let me put this question to him. When did the Canadian government first become aware that Iraq was not satisfied with the cars? Further, what steps did the government take to ensure that the Canadian taxpayer would not end up footing a bill for $80 million?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if my memory serves me correctly, I was informed some time during last summer. I then arranged to go to Baghdad during the month of September. I think it was around the end of September or the beginning of October.
Write that one down.

We obviously had ongoing discussions with the Iraqi ambassador and the embassy even as late as six weeks ago prior to his departure for Baghdad. I also sent a note to my counterpart, the Minister of Trade for Iraq, to see if he could resolve this particular situation.
Obviously the Government of Canada does not produce cars, and I am not a mechanic myself. We had hoped that we would be successful because the Malibu, as the hon. member knows, is a very good car. It just so happened that this particular model has not worked to the customer's satisfaction.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question will also be directed to the Minister of State for International Trade. Some time ago, I asked him a question about the survival of the footwear industry. The minister is well aware of the very difficult situation now facing this industry, and that the answer is to apply the over-all quota system to leather footwear as well. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The minister knows perfectly well that the industry is in extreme difficulty. Since the matter was raised some time ago and a number of members on both sides of the House have given their support on this issue, the minister should be able to inform us today when he is finally going to give an answer to this major industry and prevent the loss of thousands of jobs. Would the minister also be able to inform us today whether, in view of the information he now has, he is willing to support the request made by the footwear industry and work together with his colleague to find a solution that will prevent the loss of jobs not only in Quebec but throughout the country?

subsubtopic: VOLUME OF JAPANESE CAR SALES IN CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for International Trade concerning the automotive industry in general. Almost one job in seven in Canada is, directly or indirectly, connected with that industry. These involve workers in plastics, iron, and the fabrication of all kinds of finished products and all kinds of minerals. I ask the minister, since at this point 22 per cent of that market has been taken over by Japanese products, why does the government not have in place a requirement that Japanese firms either purchase parts or assemble vehicles here in Canada, which would put Canadians to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subsubtopic: VOLUME OF JAPANESE CAR SALES IN CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, we are very cognizant of and concerned about the situation in the automobile industry in Canada. That is one of the reasons we undertook the recent trade mission to Japan and asked the Japanese government for three possible areas of voluntary restraint: one, with respect to importation of automobiles during the current fiscal year; second, a ceiling with respect to commercial vehicles; third, a commitment to negotiate a content proposal for the future.
The negotiations are still ongoing and, as the hon. member knows, the Japanese government announced yesterday they have come to a decision with respect to the United States, and hopefully our recommendations will now be their first priority.

subtopic: DEFICIT IN AUTOMOTIVE TRADE WITH JAPAN
DEFICIT IN AUTOMOTIVE TRADE WITH JAPAN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the countries of France, Mexico, Australia and the United States, as well as a number of others, have firm agreements with the Japanese respecting either quotas or production within their countries of parts for Japanese vehicles. Considering that we have an automotive trade deficit with Japan of $1.5 billion, representing a net loss of 15,000 Canadian jobs, why is it that, unlike other countries which have protected their automotive industries, the Government of Canada has been so gutless in its dealings with Japan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subtopic: DEFICIT IN AUTOMOTIVE TRADE WITH JAPAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member forgets for a second that we are one of the few countries in the world which has a trade surplus with Japan. While most of the countries the hon. member mentioned have a substantial trade deficit with Japan, we have a $400 million trade surplus. France, for example, has
Oral Questions
severe restrictions on Japanese automobiles; however it only sells the Japanese $1 billion worth of goods. We happen to sell them over $4 billion worth.

Is the minister prepared to get at least as tough as some of these other countries are in protecting their automotive industries, and will he within a matter of weeks get a specific commitment from the Japanese either to produce parts or vehicles here, which would be fair for the Canadian consumer as well as the auto worker, or, if not, will he have the courage to tell the Japanese he is going to put an emergency 15 per cent surcharge on all their automotive products coming into Canada?

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Revenue Canada is asking Canadians to pay their 1981 taxes based on the November, 1981, budget, as if that budget were law today. The department has issued a bulletin to that effect. The minister knows full well that his phantom budget is a subject of great uncertainty today because no legislation has been presented on

March 30, 1982
Oral Questions
the budget, and there has not even been a Ways and Means motion in connection with the many changes that he has announced with regard to the budget itself. Why is the minister asking Canadians to pay their taxes based on the budget when the legislation has not even been made public?
Disgrace!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Ways and Means motions have been made public, and it is on that basis that taxes have been collected in this country for ever and a day.
They have not been voted on.

Madam Speaker, there has never been a budget in this country which has been the subject of so much uncertainty as this particular one. We have not seen the Ways and Means motion for the December 18 changes. I remind the minister of that fact. This particular request is in contempt of Parliament. The minister has limited the rights of Parliament to consider, debate and vote on the particular motions. The minister made a further withdrawal yesterday by stating that he would introduce draft legislation on the sales tax changes and allow many companies to present their views on those particular changes. Why is he allowing companies to make representations on the sales tax proposals when he has precluded and pre-empted Canadians and Parliament from discussion of the regular tax changes which were introduced in the budget?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there has been no effort to preclude discussion on the budgetary changes which were made on November 12. I believe that no budget has been subjected to such a large amount of discussion throughout the country. I know of no other budget in the history of Canada which has been brought before the House three times by the opposition in non-confidence motions and which has been approved three times. Therefore it has been extensively discussed. We will produce-
We have not seen the legislation.

speechtext: -draft legislation which will be discussed and considered by all hands. If the hon. member had consulted with the hon. member for St. John's West, he would have received that information without showing his lack of knowledge on the floor of the House.
That is a falsehood.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. The Canadian car rental industry has made the claim that the capital cost allowance item in the November 12 budget has caused the postponement of some 40,000 new cars. The 250 per cent tax increase in the taxable benefits item in the new budget has caused the further cancellation and postponement of many thousands of new cars and a loss of thousands of man-years of work. I am wondering if this minister can acquaint us with the negotiations, and with representations he has made to his colleague, the Minister of Finance, concerning the removal of these two job-destroying items in the November 12 budget?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Madam Speaker, some months ago I did meet with a delegation representing the Canadian car rental industry. I certainly took steps to see that its concerns were brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance. It is my impression that the Minister of Finance has made announcements in response to the concerns of the car rental people, particularly with respect to an analysis of some of their major concerns about the capital cost allowance. They indicated that their concerns were certainly not as severe as they first feared.

Madam Speaker, although this minister is on record as saying that he would resign from a government that allowed interest rates to increase, he is also on record as committing very large sums of money to protect jobs in troubled industries. But his best efforts to protect jobs have been wiped out by these two items in the budget. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Regional Economic Expansion should normally be outraged at this contradictory economic policy. I am going to ask him in all seriousness if he will resign now in protest over this contradiction in government economic policy.

subsubtopic: ACTION TAKEN AGAINST EMPLOYEE OF DEPARTMENT OF MANPOWER AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
I have a question, Madam Speaker, for the Minister of Employment and Immigration on the rules governing his department's employees. The minister must be aware of the unfortunate case of his departmental employee, Paul McNeill, who, like Neil Fraser, dared to express his opinion but who has a family to support and cannot risk loss of employment. He has spent $12,000 to remove urea formaldehyde foam insulation from his home in Halifax and believes the government has a responsibility, and I agree with him.
Would the minister explain why action was taken by his officials against Mr. McNeill for expressing the widely held view on government responsibility for UFFI? Would he tell the House whether he thinks the sweeping provisions of his department's Code of Conduct are justified in a free and democratic society?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: ACTION TAKEN AGAINST EMPLOYEE OF DEPARTMENT OF MANPOWER AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, the code of conduct is a set of guidelines for the activity of public servants in a department. Those guidelines were simply drawn to the attention of the gentleman in question, reminding him that that is the code of conduct of which he was aware before he accepted his present position and employment. They were simply drawn to his attention, and he could then draw his own conclusions as to whether he wanted to proceed with his activities in the private organization he was sponsoring, or whether he would continue in terms of his own activities in that department. speechtext: I think I can assist the hon. member by reminding her now that what she considers to be a misleading statement by a minister or by another member of the House does not necessarily constitute a question of privilege; it is often a matter of debate. speechtext:
This becomes a little difficult, Madam Speaker. Since the recent changes, the rules have not precluded a question of privilege from being raised during question period. A practice has developed since the recent changes where questions of privilege and points of order have been deferred until after the question period is over. It is totally irrelevant, in my submission, that the statement made by the minister was made in an area which does not concern her jurisdiction.
I might cite as a precedent in that connection the incident that gave rise to the minister's statement in the first place. It was a question and a supplementary put by the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) in connection with statements made by the minister in a speech. At that time the Chair permitted both questions and both answers.
That is where the difficulty started. The minister is now on the official record of the proceedings of this House as having made statements which the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands wishes to question. Indeed, she cites the intervention of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). We have two ministers of the Crown, both in this place, saying totally different things.
The question of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands would surely be a proper one, directed as it was to the minister and asking whether she was going to allow her misleading statement to stand. Is that a statement that exposes the government's position or is the correct statement the one made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development?
In terms of the question before the Chair, surely that has nothing to do with ministerial responsibility in the particular portfolio she or he holds; it has to do with the accuracy, indeed the validity, of statements made to members in this House. Not only has the questioner a right to put the question, but it would seem to me that the minister has an obligation to
Privilege-Miss MacDonald
answer. The question can only be put to someone on the government benches and it can only be answered by the minister who made the statement. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development cannot answer for the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether something that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has said is true or needs correction. Surely it is only the minister who made the statement who can make the necessary correction.

speechtext:
In so far as the Department of External Affairs is concerned, the answer is as follows:
1. The financial accounts with respect to the operations of the ICSC are the responsibility of India as the designated administering power under the Geneva agreements. India presented a final statement of account, including recoverable
costs incurred by Canada, to the co-chairmen of the 1954 Geneva Conference-the United Kingdom and the U.S.S.R.- in 1973. An appeal was subsequently addressed to the contributors-the United Kingdom, France, the U.S.S.R., the People's Republic of China and the Democratic Republic of Viet Nam-to settle the outstanding debts of the commission, including those owed to the member powers, by financial contributions to the common fund. This appeal, as was the case with previous appeals dating back to commencement of the commission, was not responded to by all of the contributing powers. As a result, the accounts remain open until such time as the contributing powers meet their financial obligations.
2.	The total cost of the operation for Canada was $10,509,000 of which $5,573,000 was non-recoverable and $4,936,000 was recoverable. The total cost of the operations for the three supervisory powers is not known as we do not have access to the complete records of expenditures for India and Poland.
3.	The contributing powers to the common fund set up for the Viet Nam and Cambodia Commissions-the United Kingdom, the U.S.S.R., France and the People's Republic of China-were responsible for 25 per cent each of the costs. The contributing powers to the commission for Laos and their respective financial responsibilities are: People's Republic of China, France, United Kingdom, U.S.A. and U.S.S.R. (17.6 per cent); Burma, Cambodia, Laos, North Viet Nam, South Viet Nam, Thailand (1.5 per cent); Canada, India, Poland (1 per cent). The precise contributions of countries other than Canada are not available from our records.
4.	The common fund is considered the administrative debtor for funds owed to the participating countries in the ICSCs and the contributing powers have a collective responsibility to meet the financial obligations to the fund. Certain contributing powers have made no contributions to the fund (People's Republic of China, Democratic Republic of Viet Nam) and have never evinced any desire to meet their financial obligations.
5 and 6. Various efforts have been made to have the contributing powers meet their financial obligations to the common fund, but these have not been received with any enthusiasm. Canada has made various direct approaches to the Indian government, the governments of the contributing powers and the co-chairmen of the 1954 Geneva Conference regarding reimbursement of the outstanding amounts- $3,208,043-owed to Canada. Our last official demarches were made in 1978 but the subject has been brought up informally from time to time since then by our embassy in Moscow and our high commission in London. We are not optimistic that the amounts owing either to Canada or to the other participants will be recovered but the accounts remain open and further efforts will be made to obtain reimbursement.

The House resumed from Monday, March 29, consideration of Bill C-88, respecting loans to farmers, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Agriculture; and Motion No. 1 (Mr. Hamilton, Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain).

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on this bill, I want to bring to the attention of the House two or three things that I think are quite significant. First, I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has not fulfilled his responsibility in the manner in which he could have and should have. Certainly there has been a real lack of imagination on his part. This is evidenced by the lack of programming that has taken place and the lack of interest that he has portrayed by not doing the things required in order to have a healthy agricultural community in Canada. You can have the most productive land in the world and you can have the best farmers in the world, Mr. Speaker, but unless the government sets the climate for continuing production, production which the world requires, then the agricultural industry and those involved in it will suffer as a consequence.
Over the last ten years I feel that the agricultural community in Canada has suffered great neglect as a result of the administration of the present Minister of Agriculture. I well remember when he first took office. He said that he was going to be a minister of agriculture who answered the phone. I think that about all he has done over the years is answer the phone. Unfortunately, no one else has filled the vacancy created by the minister while he answers the phone. While I recognize the importance of this bill, which will supply more funding to the farmers all across Canada, nevertheless that is not the answer to the agricultural problems in Canada today.
We have a government which seems to be ever incessant in its tax demands. It places the burden on those people who are producing and who are working, but fewer and fewer people are carrying the load. My first question, then, to the minister and to members opposite is this: is anyone listening? Does

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
anyone actually know what has happened? The warning flags are out and Members of Parliament better realize that. Farmers and those in the agricultural industry are slipping further and further into debt. Sure, we get extra financing for a short time, but this financing is at an ever-increasing rate of interest. High interest costs are causing the problems facing the farming community. Those of us who have many farmers in our constituencies recognize that last summer the crunch started to come when interest rates escalated to an all-time Canadian high. It was at that time that farmers got into trouble. Farmers were prepared to carry a reasonable rate of interest, say 10 per cent or 11 per cent, but once interest rates got up into the high teens and low twenties, that is when their serious problems commenced. Farmers had to start selling off parts of their farming operations. That is why the situation is so serious, and that is why I say that the warning flags are out.
I would venture to say that this year the net income of agricultural producers will be down 25 per cent. That is a 25 per cent drop simply because the input costs of those involved in the agricultural industry will rise somewhere between 10 per cent and 15 per cent.
I will explain and give one example to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the House, of where the government is responsible for some of the cost. I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) yesterday whether he would consider abolishing the excise tax on home heating fuels, natural gas and home heating oil. Farmers also have to heat their homes just like all other consumers in Canada.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says we have to bring prices down to control inflation. We agree with him about that. We agree with the Prime Minister that inflation has to be controlled. But you have to recognize it was the same Prime Minister who told us some seven years ago that inflation was wrestled to the ground. Where is inflation today compared to seven years ago? Inflation is running rampant. The government does not know how to handle a situation like this. Yet the government is adding to inflation by levying an extra excise tax on fuel for home heating, such as natural gas and oil.
There are farmers in our area whose costs to heat their poultry houses, their hog barns and their homes are $1,000 a month. Almost one third of that cost is going into the federal coffers through excise tax. It would seem to me that if the Minister of Agriculture had any clout or if there was any desire on the part of those in the cabinet to improve the situation, one of the things they would want to do would be to refrain from placing an extra burden on those in the productive end of agriculture. Why can the government not bring costs down? Why do we have to have extra burdens placed on those people who are trying to produce and who are working longer hours perhaps than any other sector of our community? Yet the government will not see fit to cut back on that tax.
I want to tell you something else, Mr. Speaker. Many rural communities have natural gas supplied by co-ops which they have set up and are running themselves. These co-ops have to collect this tax. At the present time the government will not wait a reasonable length of time, say 90 days, for that tax. We have discussed this 90-day collection time before in the House.
I am sure that if you had your way, Mr. Speaker, the message would get through to the cabinet and they would wait at least 90 days before requiring money from the co-operatives. But no, the Minister of Finance said yesterday he is not prepared to change that tax at the present time. To me that is totally unacceptable. It is not realistic to require co-operatives to pay money over before they collect it. Because of that requirement, the co-operatives have a continuous loan in the vicinity of $100,000. I do not think that is just, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you do not either.

The problem, Mr. Speaker, is that members opposite cannot face the truth. I said earlier that the farming community is going to have a drop of approximately 25 per cent in their net income this year. This is really serious because it is going to put an extra strain on their finances. At the present time the price of beef and pork is down 10 per cent to 15 per cent. Barley is down about $1 a bushel, and wheat is down about $2. So how can we expect the farming community to cope with this 10 per cent or 15 per cent increase in the cost of production? Because that is what it is. They are caught in the squeeze and we have a government which will not move even a little to help them.
Why should we bring in legislation to increase production costs, which is what is happening with the increase in the gasoline tax? We have to remember, Mr. Speaker, that our producers have to compete with the United States, and at the present time the price of gasoline there is approximately 10 per cent or 15 per cent less than here. We are putting producers in a strait-jacket, and it is totally unacceptable.
I do not like statistics, Mr. Speaker, but I am going to put some on record to show the current situation in the agricultural industry. I am glad to see the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell), the former premier of one of our great provinces, is here listening to this debate because I know his province's economy depends a great deal on agriculture. Repayment arrears to the Farm Credit Corporation are increasing in all provinces with the exception of British Columbia. Compared to 1980, the arrears for 1981 in Alberta increased from 8.7 per cent to 9.7 per cent; in Saskatchewan, 6.1 per cent to 7.3 per cent; Manitoba, 5.5 per cent to 9.1 per cent; Ontario, 5.9 per cent to 7.6 per cent; Quebec, 6.1 per cent to 9 per cent; New Brunswick, 8.9 per cent to 11.2 per cent;

Nova Scotia, 9.6 per cent to 12.8 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 8.9 per cent to 10.7 per cent; Newfoundland, 30.6 per cent to 35.9 per cent. The over-all average increase was from 6.7 per cent to 8.3 per cent.
That is the trend, Mr. Speaker. Farmers are delaying their repayments with the result that there is not as much money to lend out as there should be. Therefore, we have to recognize there is a problem out there, it is increasing, and these changes to the FCC will not really have that much effect on the overall operation of the corporation or the farming community.
One of the fears I have concerning this bill is the suggestion made by the Minister of Agriculture in committee when he said that perhaps the corporation could go to Switzerland to borrow cheap money. Mr. Speaker, I want to warn the government and the farmer that what may be cheap money today may not be so cheap down the road. If rumours of depreciation of the dollar ever materialize, those loans will no longer be cheap. I would far rather have the Minister of Agriculture accept the amendment of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and allow the FCC to borrow money within our own economic community. The money might come from farmers selling their farms, or they might have had a good year with extra money available which they could put into the FCC and not have to pay tax on until such time as they are ready. There might be other groups or individuals who are prepared to do the same thing. It is a great way to Canadianize the system. Far better to do that than to try and Canadianize some of those Swiss banks.
The attempt by this government to Canadianize the industry is one of the reasons we now have higher energy costs than the United States. A great portion of the funding for this program comes out of the agricultural community because farmers use a lot of energy. A lot of their tax dollars are being siphoned off to buy oil companies which are not going to find or produce another barrel of oil, and I do not think they are going to make oil any cheaper. In fact, if we recognize what some Crown corporations have done to Canada, they will in fact increase the cost to the consumer.
I think the minister is on the wrong track by not accepting the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. The only excuse the Minister of Agriculture could give us last night for not accepting this amendment was that his advisers were against it. Well, for goodness sakes! Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill today. I come from a riding which is a very rich agricultural area, especially in the southern and western parts. When I read the history of my area, the riding of Victoria-Haliburton, I could understand why the early settlers came there. They arrived by water and by land, and they undertook to clear this very fertile soil and to make homes for their families for generations to come. We do have some industry. We have a mixed riding. Today I want to discuss the agricultural industry. There are a number of farmers in my riding who are in milk and grain production, and in every other segment of the agricultural industry.
There are a number of features in this bill with which I agree. I might even say that some of them are long overdue. However, considering the state of the agricultural industry in Canada, I would have to ask if this bill is too late to be truly effective in revitalizing the agricultural industry. This bill would have to be implemented in tandem with a policy of low interest rates. All hon. members in this House are aware, even those who are not directly involved in agriculture, that high interest rates are killing off the farms at a rate not seen in our country since the great depression.
I am encouraged by the provisions of this bill which would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to advance loans to nonfarmers who can provide a plan indicating they would become viable within five years. However, unless we can provide some assurance that they will remain on their farms for five years or more, Bill C-88 will be just another exercise in futility. What chance will they have to survive if farmers of long experience and of proven good management are selling out, some for small profits and others just to cut their losses? There were more than 8,000 farm failures in 1981, a large percentage of which were bankruptcies. A vast majority involved experienced farmers.
I want to see more people, especially young people, getting started in farming. For some people it is the only way of life they want. However, almost every day people tell me that they simply cannot afford the large down payment required today, mostly due to the provisions in the November 1981 budget concerning capital gains reserves and income averaging annuity contracts. After a lifetime of hard work, looking forward to the day when he can retire in comfort, the farmer of today must get a large down payment on the sale of his farm just to pay the capital gains tax, a tax on money he hoped to collect in the future.
There are some aspects of this bill which farmers can applaud, although not too loudly. There is no indication in Bill C-88 that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) are on the same wavelength. One giveth and the other taketh away. The Minister of Agriculture has been reported as saying that the Farm Credit Corporation will have $1 billion to lend out by June of this year. I notice that this bill will authorize the

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
corporation to obtain a total of $350 million from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This is based on a formula whereby the corporation would be able to obtain from the government 25 times its capitalization of $14 million.
Let us assume that the Farm Credit Corporation fund will be swollen by an additional $150 million this year through payments by mortgage holders. This would make a total of $500 million available to the Farm Credit Corporation to make new loans. What would be the source of the other $500 million? It would presumably be through the provisions of Clause 8 of this bill which revises Section 13 of the Farm Credit Act. This revised section would authorize the Farm Credit Corporation, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, to borrow money by any means, including the issuing and selling of bonds, debentures, notes and other evidence of the indebtedness of the corporation.
Under subsection (2) we find that the Minister of Finance may lend the Farm Credit Corporation money out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. So far, so good. But we then come to subsection (3), which states that the aggregate amount outstanding pursuant to subsections (1) and (2) shall not at any time exceed 25 times the capital of the corporation. By my calculations, this brings us back to the $500 million, not the $1 billion trotted out by the Minister of Agriculture.
I would like some assurance from the minister that this is not some more of the razzle-dazzle practised so skilfully by the Minister of Finance. I would like to have some assurance from the Minister of Agriculture that the $350 million from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, plus the $150 million payment from mortgage holders, will be separate and distinct from the corporation's authorization to borrow money on the market.
There is also the question of what rates of interest will apply where funds other than those from the Consolidated Revenue Fund are loaned by the Farm Credit Corporation. Funds raised through bonds and debentures will command a higher rate of interest than the rate presently charged by the Farm Credit Corporation. There is nothing in this bill to indicate whether these higher rates of interest will be subsidized by the federal government.
I am not too pleased with Clause 14 of this bill. It authorizes the Farm Credit Corporation to keep its funds and accounts in the Bank of Canada and other financial institutions in and out of Canada. I think it should state "any financial institution in Canada", period.
I would like to go back for a moment to the question of the presumed authorization of the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow money on the open market. I think that some clarification of this section is called for. However, let us assume that the corporation does float bonds and debentures on the money market. I would like to see some provision in this bill whereby the Farm Credit Corporation would be able to issue bonds such as the Small Business Development Bond and that the interest be made tax deductible. If it works for business it should work for the farmer.
I certainly go along with the phrase of the Minister of Agriculture quoted yesterday by the member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), when the minister stated that the future of agriculture is ahead of us. I believe that, Mr. Speaker, and I also believe in the interest of the Minister of Agriculture. I think he tries. Probably he is not getting the support he should. I have found in my dealings with the Minister of Agriculture that I always get along very well with him. He has been very receptive. We meet and we chat quite often. But I think the government has a responsibility to our agricultural industry, the oldest industry that has a future in Canada, if it is managed properly by the department and encouraged.
The interest rate the farmer has to pay today to obtain conventional loans from the bank makes it absolutely impossible for him to borrow money and carry on. This is what is hurting our farming community probably more than anything else. It is also hurting every other industry. It leaves the farmer very uncompetitive in a market that fluctuates up and down.
Another point is that the return the farmer receives on his product is going down. The attitude of the banking industry toward the farmer and the agricultural industry is such that over 8,000 farmers last year had to declare bankruptcy. There probably will be many more. This is something our country cannot afford.
Our farmers are faced on practically every product with a decrease in their returns. This is something they may have to take for granted. When they go to the bank to arrange a loan-which is practically a necessity with every farmer today, not all but the vast majority of them-and when they go to sell their product, they are not sure what they will get for it on the market.
Many farmers come to me with their problems, and I can recall a few of them. In one case I might mention, the farm was handed down from father to son for generations. As the method of farming changed, the son who inherited the farm was forced to buy new machinery. He was forced to go, as some people would say, "mod" if he wanted to stay in existence. He goes to the Farm Credit Corporation; he goes to his bank; he borrows money. He has no idea that there will be an increase in interest rates three years down the road. Probably he was underfinanced by the Farm Credit Corporation. They gave him all kinds of advice, that he had to buy a certain type of machinery to be successful or he would not get a loan, or he had to increase his production of whatever the commodity may have been or he would not qualify for a loan. He would not have the cash flow. Today, not only have the returns and the cash flow gone down, but his interest rate has gone up. It leaves him in a very tight position.
When he goes back to the Farm Credit Corporation, he is told, "You are doing things all in the wrong way; your cash flow is not high enough". What is this man to do? He can get no more money from his bank. The Farm Credit Corporation should, to my mind, give him more money. I know there are
March 30, 1982

exceptions; I will not stand here and say there are not. There are exceptions. But there also should be consideration. The Farm Credit Corporation should be acting to promote the agricultural industry. Its goal is the betterment of the agricultural industry, but it is letting this farmer down. He is going to lose the family farm; he has teenage daughters going to school; he has a small family; he is going to go through the embarrassment of asking, "How many lives is this going to ruin?"
How many people that make that decision in respect of this gentleman have to worry about their pay cheque? I think some of our people representing probably every segment of our government, those who have to deal with the real world of people, are not understanding enough. They are too inconsiderate; they go out with a blank piece of paper and forms and regulations. There is no end to it.
Also the farmer, if he is successful, probably has to wait. I had a phone call this morning. A young farmer who had over $70,000 collateral to put up and who wanted to borrow $40,000 to increase his farm machinery for custom work-I will deal with that in a moment-goes to the Farm Credit Corporation and is told he has to wait six weeks before they would even look at his case. That is what he had to do. Imagine waiting six weeks in the spring of the year before he can have his case even considered! This man is a proven farmer and a very aggressive farmer. We should have a more positive approach and a more understandable approach by all our representatives-and I do not stop just at the Farm Credit Corporation. After all is said and done, they are civil servants, they are there to serve their fellow men as well as being representatives of the government. Of late, 1 have had too many complaints about the standoffish attitude of some who are filling these positions. They are not a credit to the department.
I certainly go along with the remarks of the member from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain who moved this motion. He is a positive thinker. There are many suggestions he offered, not only this amendment but in his speech last night, that the minister should take into consideration. I think the minister will take these into consideration.
I wish to stress again, my friends, that the farmer is finding himself in dire straits. We have to look on the farmer today as a businessman. He is a businessman. When we see that the Japanese farmer can borrow money at 3.5 per cent interest, how does this stack up with our Canadian farmer who is paying anywhere from 17 per cent to 20 per cent interest, of the preferred rate which I think is now 16.25 per cent from the Farm Credit Corporation?
We are neglecting our farmers. We have a commodity here, my friends, that we will not have to worry about on the world markets. We should be catering to a hungry world, for we find hunger in many parts of the world. This is an industry the products of which will always be in demand.
So I appeal to the minister to take into consideration the lending practices of the Farm Credit Corporation and to ensure there is a little bit of understanding on the part of those people who represent him throughout the country.
Farm Loans
I heard the minister say yesterday in respect of farm credit corporations that if they were given too much range with respect to the principle of the Small Business Development Bond the money supply for other industry would dry up. I need only think back to last November when the Government of Canada borrowed bond money from Canadians at 19'/2 per cent interest. That dried up a lot of money for businesses. Yesterday the minister talked of the money that was available to him and the Farm Credit Corporation. I would encourage the minister to secure as much of that money as possible and make it available to our farmers in Canada so that they can eke out an existence in a healthy agricultural community.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to speak on this bill amending the Farm Credit Act. Probably no area of the economy is more affected by the vagaries of the marketplace than farming. Only in agriculture is the market system still expected to work. Only the farmer is expected to put his product on the shelf and accept what is offered. The idea that supply and demand, the open market, will dictate how much a farmer will make is as outmoded as the walking plough. However, some still believe it is the panacea for the industry.
Bill C-88 before us is concerned with the survival of the farmer. I state it that way because it is important that we emphasize the end result of not providing the farm community with the kinds of programs which allow it to survive in a more natural way. I could spend a considerable amount of time developing a scenario about the need for credit to survive. Unfortunately, the Farm Credit Corporation has become an agency which controls to some extent the hope of survival for many farmers.
It is a pretty good indication of the ineffectiveness of our agricultural policy when we must recognize that the Farm Credit Corporation, which was originally set up to assist farmers to develop and grow, has become an agency of survival, and it is not doing too well at that. When you look at the bankruptcy rates and the number of liquidations, you can see that the corporation is not doing particularly well in helping farmers to survive. We now have a situation where the corporation which was set up for development has become the corporation to which farmers look to survive.
During the last week a group of Ontario farmers visited Ottawa. I am sure many members here met with them. They call themselves the Canadian Farmers' Survival Association. That group indicated that thousands of farmers will not survive the next couple of months.
Yesterday my colleague from Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) read into the record the recommendations which that group made when they were here. Ideally, if farmers generally are given the kind of policy and security they should have, we would not have to be looking at amendments to the Farm Credit Act. There would be no increase in debt. As it is, their indebtedness is steadily increasing. I again refer to my
15964

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
colleague's speech where he indicated the level in the change of debt over the past ten years.
In considering the need for farm credit, we should examine the capacity of the farm community to borrow. Canadian farmers have been a very good bet for the lending agencies. The repayment rates under various federal programs are invariably outstanding. The records of the Farm Credit Corporation and the Canadian Wheat Board will attest to that. Further, Canadian farmers are not over their heads as far as the total debt carried is concerned.
A 1981 farm survey conducted by the Farm Credit Corporation showed that Canadian farmers had 85 per cent equity on average net assets of something over $400,000. This indicates that farmers have the capacity to carry farm credit if it is available for long terms and at interest rates that are less than usurious.
Until a few years ago, any rate over 6 per cent was considered usury. It then went to 12 per cent and more recently operating loans for farmers have been at 23 per cent. As interest rates tripled between 1977 and 1981, one need hardly ask why a credit-intensive industry such as farming has got into so much difficulty. Clearly the difficulty in the farming community is related not to the ability to produce but to borrowing capacity.
Since the Government of Canada is supposed to be the lender of last resort, when talking about the problems of lending we must talk about the problems of the Government of Canada. In many discussions on farm credit, myths have been propounded by people who should know better. One myth has been the criticism of the banks which say that a shortage of money is not the problem but rather poor farming practices. That criticism of farmers by the lending institutions is a myth.
Every Member of Parliament who lives in an agricultural riding knows it is not correct. Case after case is brought to our attention by sound applicants who have been turned down by the banks or discouraged from applying for small business bonds. They have been turned down for a limited amount of farm credit by the Farm Credit Corporation emergency fund. They are seeking any kind of financing just to be able to keep on farming.
The actual number of farm bankruptcies filed in the bankruptcy branch of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in 1979 was 125. That number is fairly small, given that there are more than 300,000 farmers in Canada. Yet the year to year increase in bankruptcies is significant, and the percentage increases are staggering. In 1979 there were 125. In 1980 there were 222, an increase of 77.6 per cent. In 1981 there were 261, an increase of 17.6 per cent. We recently received a report on the first two months of 1982, and according to that report the total for those two months was 63, an increase of 54 per cent over the same two months in 1981. Clearly the increase in farm bankruptcies has not stopped, regardless of what the bankers of Canada say or what little the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) does.
The second myth about farmers is that they are all rich and do not need increased farm credit. A recent study by George L. Brinkman for the Economic Council of Canada entitled "Farm Income in Canada" tried to show the profitability of Canadian farms. The study pointed out that if capital appreciation is taken into account, farms have profitability similar to businesses of a similar size. Yet farmers know, as do most hon. members here this afternoon-it is too bad the economists do not know-that capital gain does not produce cash for expenses and credit for investment. Assets can be liquidated, but liquidation also means the viability of a farm is likely to be in question. Further, fixed assets on a farm are only valuable if someone wants to buy them, and that is not always the case in areas where agriculture may be a depressed industry.
The group which visited us last week, the Canadian Farmers' Survival Association, pointed out to us that in some areas of Ontario the price of land, which was running at $1,000 an acre last year or the year before, has dropped to $250 an acre, so even fixed assets become a liability.
Most of us who have examined Bill C-88 have come away with the feeling that it does not meet the major test for longterm credit legislation and that it does not provide reasonable amounts of money at reasonable cost repayable over a ten-year term or longer. Farm Credit Corporation money currently costs 16.75 per cent, and that level might be increased if what the Minister of Agriculture suggests should be the basis for borrowing is in effect. Yet within this bill there does not seem to be any guarantee that the Farm Credit Corporation will be able to borrow at the same rate as government bonds which, at the moment, is 1.25 per cent lower than the 16.75 per cent the Farm Credit Corporation is charging.
Historically the Farm Credit Corporation has always trailed the prime rate offered by the chartered banks. In the 19771981 period the gap was about 1.65 per cent. There does not appear to be any guarantee in this bill which would maintain the historical difference between Farm Credit Corporation and bank prime rates. Perhaps the minister should consider giving a guarantee that Farm Credit Corporation rates will continue to track below the prime rates charged by the banks or, because his policies have been so inadequate in the funding of farms in the past and in keeping the level of income high enough to survive, perhaps the minister should guarantee a level much lower than that. Perhaps he should guarantee a level of 3.5 per cent, which would be somewhat of a service rate in the lending of money to farmers who are having problems. In his speech yesterday the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) suggested that it might be possible to have a rate of one-half prime. Any of these proposals would be much better than what is in the bill now; the bill makes it possible for Farm Credit Corporation loans to cost more than bank loans in the future.
A second criticism many of us have raised concerns longterm credit in general. Is credit truly long term if the bank has the option of converting a loan into a demand note with a
March 30, 1982

floating rate? That does not seem to me to fill the requirement of long-term credit at a fixed rate.
I note in this Farm Credit Corporation bill that there is a bit of wandering about in relation to trying to establish ten years as a possible term for a fixed rate. It is striking to note that the government is considering getting out of the business of longterm loans to farmers. The Farm Credit Corporation was the traditional supplier of more than 70 per cent of long-term credit; now it supplies 20 per cent. The gap in the marketplace has been filled, of course, by the banks, but banks-particularly the Canadian chartered banks-do not enter the lending field without throwing their weight around.
We saw that most recently when the Canadian Farmers' Survival Association visited our caucus. In its five-point plan the association wanted the reinstatement of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act of 1934. That request was a serious request. That legislation served the purpose of giving farmers economic security in return for the socially and economically desirable activity of providing food for Canadians. However, what was the response of the Minister of Agriculture? He said we cannot bring that law back because if we brought it back, that would frighten the banks out of agricultural lending. It is not good enough that farmers have shown outstanding ability to repay their loans; the banks still had to be able to foreclose, if they wished, before they would consider lending to farmers.
I am pleased that the survival association continues to help the farmers. I may not agree with its methods in every case but at least it is attempting to help. I commend its motto, "Never negotiate out of fear but never fear to negotiate," to the Minister of Agriculture.
In many ways it appears that partial privatization through the Farm Credit Corporation is the way the government wants agriculture to go today. The Farm Credit Corporation has been a rather underworked agency in recent years. In the peak lending years, 1965 to 1968, between 10,000 and 12,000 loans were granted, but in 1981 under 5,000 loans were granted. If the government can convince me that privatization will come close to meeting the demand and that it may have a case for taking this step-

The government does not claim that the privatization of the Farm Credit Corporation will solve the problem; rather, it
Farm Loans
claims that in time, as the mechanisms for borrowing are put in place and the corporation establishes itself in the financial markets, a progressively larger portion of its funds could be obtained directly from that source. The government is suggesting that it is going to get out of this entirely and that this action will therefore force the corporation to become a private organization lending money at the going rate. speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-88, respecting loans to farmers, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Agriculture; and Motion No. 1 (Mr. Hamilton, Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain).

subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). I think a number of different things should be dealt with as we debate the bill, which will be discussed further on third reading, and that a little bit of background would help put the whole bill, and specifically the amendment, in context. The amendment is the key to the whole bill. I will try to expand upon some of the points that have already been dealt with by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain in his remarks.

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
The first point I would raise is the terrific interest that the government shows in this legislation. I know it is not the decent thing to criticize the government, but 1 would like to honour those members of the opposition parties who have participated in the debate. They have brought forward important points and issues that affect agriculture today. I regret that those members of the government who represent rural ridings have not participated more actively.
People who are facing the loss of their jobs in the auto industry or those involved in business or some economic activity may be wondering whether farming deserves all the attention it gets and whether farmers are worse off than many other segments of the economy. It is important to point out, however, that this is a primary industry. Whatever happens in farming, as in forestry and mining, for instance, has significant repercussions throughout the economy. The multiplier effect- whether that would be seven or any other figure-generates wealth in the economy. It has been a traditional base in Canada. We are in danger of losing a significant portion of that base, Mr. Speaker.
We have learned that Canadians are paying more in taxes than they are for food or shelter. At the very least, that raises the question of the level of taxation, whether on oil, gas or fuels, that is required for agricultural production and whether the return to the farmer at the farm gate is adequate. Interest rates are a significant factor in the cost of production today. This view is supported by many farm groups.
The question of interest rates has traditionally been dealt with by the Farm Credit Corporation. In the last ten years the interest portion of agricultural production has increased by approximately 645 per cent. That is a fantastic increase, Mr. Speaker. If the farmer or the consumer compares the actual return on a pound of beef or a bushel of corn at the farm gate ten years ago with the price received today, it is evident that there has not been a six times increase in price. The increase in the interest cost is the most important single issue and the one that we have to deal with effectively and quickly if we are to maintain that base in agriculture.
The most important part of the bill appears on page 4 in Clause 13(1) which reads as follows:
The corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means, including issuing and selling bonds, debentures, notes and other evidences of indebtedness of the corporation.
The key word and the one that the amendment makes reference to is "bond". The amendment offered by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain reads as follows:
That Bill C-88, an act respecting loans to farmers, be amended in Clause 8 by adding immediately after line 31 at page 4 the following:
"(1.1) For greater certainty, the expression 'bonds' referred to in subsection
(1) includes 'small business development bond'."
Members of the New Democratic Party have suggested that this measure could be more appropriately dealt with by the taxation department, and perhaps that is so. But the point is that the concept be understood and accepted by the lawyers acting for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on this amendment-and he had a little trouble with that yesterdayand that the concept of the bond be understood, de facto, to be a part of the new legislation as it affects farm credit.
When we consider that different people look at the question in different ways, we must remember the bottom line. Whether it is individual lenders to the Farm Credit Corporation or lending institutions that lend money to individual farmers, they use the principle where, through taxation devices, there is an opportunity for borrowers to have effective rates of interest which are considerably lower than those prevailing through the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada, as described and in fact dictated by government policy.
The situation now, whether interest rates are 10 per cent or 25 per cent, as they have been, is that we cannot afford at the agricultural level to continue paying those costs and expect agriculture to survive. If we look at Japan and a number of other countries, we see that they are able with a number of devices to take advantage of significantly lower rates. We are forced in world markets, and even in domestic ones, to compete with those different producers. Perhaps the United States is the best example of a country which is able to produce with the advantage of low interest rates as part of its cost of production.
Other amendments have been proposed. The one proposed by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is in part the same idea as the amendment about which we are talking now. I should like to quote from the presentation of Mr. Kirk on behalf of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, wherein he said that the federation would like an amendment to change the title of the act from:
-an act to provide for the extension of long-term mortgages to farmers to an act to extend short-intermediate and long-term credit services to the farmers.
The bond principle can be applied in a number of ways. It could be a short-term bond. In fact, the legislation could be drafted in many ways. Recently I talked with representatives of the Bank of Montreal who indicated that they have bonds which they are turning into ten-year time frames because they know producers cannot carry repayments on principal and interest over normal five-year periods. The bond principle can be adjusted to any number of periods of time, but the bottom line is lower interest rates if we are to achieve the goals which in fact are necessary at this time.
The key point made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was that indeed the situation was very difficult because long-term capital had not been provided at reasonable interest rates. There is an immediate problem today, not tomorrow. Over the past several months a problem has been brought into sharper focus, and perhaps will be brought to an unfortunate climax within the next several months, and that is that farmers need more capital, particularly operating capital, for planting. Spring planting is coming and there are a number of farmers who are now technically bankrupt. There are farmers who will not be able to borrow enough money to provide seed and fertilizer to work the land. This will have repercussions-if they do not plant, they cannot harvest. The only cash flow to
March 30, 1982

which some producers can look now is from cash crop. The short-term problem must be addressed immediately.
There has been the extraordinary appearance on the farm scene of different groups. Some are concerned farm women who are trying to address the problem and have met with both provincial and federal ministers of agriculture in Ontario. Also the Canadian Farmers' Survival Association met with Members of Parliament from all parties to bring forward its specific suggestions and concerns. No matter what is the mechanism, there is a general consensus among all farm organizations and all actively participating farmers that there must be a shortterm solution with lower interest rates.
I should like to follow my specific comments with a problem which I have experienced in the past two or three months with the Minister of Agriculture concerning the bill. This specifically refers to the amendment so I think it is quite appropriate. The minister has made a number of comments. Last Friday I looked through some of the commentaries which have been made on the agricultural scene. "Phooey on Bouey" is one quote of the Minister of Agriculture. This quotation appeared in an article by Roy MacGregor in Today. The article went on:
-"MacEachen said he was going to make the banks bleed. Hell, he gave them a transfusion".
Those comments of the Minister of Agriculture are very appealing to people who are in distress in the agricultural community, people who are facing foreclosures or receiverships, people who see interest rates continuing to climb because there is no resolution of the problem. But indeed they create confusion and should raise some serious question, if not a question of privilege in so far as the Minister of Agriculture is concerned. The minister talked about raising additional funds through private borrowing. He went so far as to say in February of this year that he would have an extra $1 billion for farmers to borrow through the Farm Credit Corporation. He commented upon this in such a manner that we should question what kind of a game he is playing with the agricultural community.
We have awaited this legislation for several years. We heard about it all last summer as the minister talked with different farm groups that were facing difficult problems. Now we have this promise finally coming off with new legislation, and we have the Minister of Agriculture talking about providing an extra $1 billion from private funding. The situation is that he is out in the country saying "Phooey on Bouey" and "Mac-Eachen has given the banks a transfusion", which are in direct contradiction to stated cabinet policy.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested that he should have resignations from people within cabinet if they do not support or choose to criticize cabinet solidarity and cabinet policy. Yet the Minister of Agriculture is out in the country doing precisely that, I hope honestly to tell the farm community what he thinks. I would be more concerned that he is doing it to placate or hoodwink them a little at the same time, because he stands up in the House and votes for the budget
Farm Loans
and the principles involved in the budget. We must take it that at least in the House he is supporting the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the high interest rate policies of the government. He cannot have it both ways. He is a pretty capable fellow at speaking out of both sides of his mouth at the same time. This is something which should be seriously questioned by the House, because I think there is a serious question of conflict. I do not know what is his ultimate purpose in doing that, but I think it does not serve any good purpose for the agricultural community or the country to be getting a number of mixed signals. I really question how honest it was for him to do it.
My final point in speaking to the amendment concerns optimism. We all know what agriculture in Canada can do. We all know that it can produce more and that there will be world markets for agricultural products. We all know that there will be large numbers of people who will have to be fed. But this optimism and indeed the hope for economic recovery and the required renewal, if we are to achieve our potential not only in agriculture but in other areas, are seriously questioned by the whole country.
I think the specific point we come down to is whether or not the Minister of Agriculture can come up with $1 billion in the short term, whether the interest rate will be satisfactory, so that farmers and capable producers will be able to survive in the long term. It is a question of whether the Minister of Agriculture will be able to get from Treasury Board the additional $26 million on top of the $14 million that has already been asked for, making the capital base sufficient to allow him to borrow that extra $1 billion. That is a serious question. From all indications we now have a situation where the Minister of Agriculture has demonstrated that he is really impotent in being able to bring forward agricultural problems to cabinet productively.
The total contribution which the federal government has made to those segments of the agricultural community that are in distress now is $5 million, and that is for the whole country. The rest is money borrowed from the Consolidated Revenue Fund which provided a program for about 135 farmers. That program finished three months ago, but that money has to be repaid. The only contribution that has been made is $5 million. The minister has said publicly that there is no way there can be any kind of stabilization for the year 1981. He is now coming up with a supply management program which may or may not be what agriculture wants. But he has been unable to bring forward the kind of support that agriculture needs at this time from cabinet.
I look forward to speaking on third reading of this bill if I have the opportunity.

In my opinion, this amendment is very straightforward and very worth while. For the life of me I cannot understand why the government does not accept it and be proud that we have someone in the House who can move an amendment which makes as much sense as this one.
What the amendment seeks to do is to make it easier for the Farm Credit Corporation to make use of the small business bond principle. That is a very simple and straightforward principle. It would aid farmers in terms of making financing available to them at a lower rate of interest. We know that interest rates are the biggest problem that faces our farmers this spring as they go to the fields to put crops in the ground enabling them to harvest this fall.
The hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) who just spoke pointed out that if you do not seed, you do not harvest. That should be obvious even to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Yet if farmers are not able to get enough financing to seed, there will be no harvest. Among other things this amendment seeks to make it easier for farmers to finance their spring operations.
What does the Minister of Agriculture tell us in response to the amendment? Last night, as reported in Hansard at page 15930, the Minister of Agriculture said:
However, because Section 13(1) does not exclude what the hon. member is suggesting, the amendment as suggested is not necessary, again according to my legal advisers. In cither case, the concept of the small business bond would require complementary amendments, I am told, of the Income Tax Act,-
My response to that is, so what? If it requires an amendment to the Income Tax Act, let us amend it. Let us not give the income tax people a chance to say that they cannot bring forward that kind of an incentive to farmers because we did not do it on this side of the House, because we did not do it with the bill in front of us. That is absolute nonsense. I think it is totally irresponsible for the Minister of Agriculture to put up that kind of what I call stupid argument against the amendment, because that is exactly what it is.
Just to emphasize what the hon. member for Bruce-Grey said, I revert to what the Minister of Agriculture said before Christmas. He said farmers are gutless, they are not doing anything. If there is ever an example of a gutless farm leader, it is the Minister of Agriculture. We have a very simple, straightforward amendment to put through but he does not even have the guts to stand up to his department. If that is the case, why have a minister of agriculture? All he has to do is say, "I am sorry, don't bother driving me around in my car, it will save the taxpayers some expense; I will just do what the department tells me to do." Why have a minister of agriculture? I think a lot of farmers are beginning to ask that question.
The minister talked about the banks. I do not know whether I can quote him exactly, but I can paraphrase him. The minister referred to the banks and some of their lending practices as being scandalous and fraudulent. You would think from that statement that if the minister had a chance to do something in terms of lowering interest rates paid to banks he
would do something about it. That is what the amendment is designed to do. Specifically, Section 13(1) will read:
The corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means,-
And the amendment is there to make sure that "by any means" specifically includes the small business development bond concept. Again, you would think that a minister who would want to accuse the banking system in this country of being fraudulent and scandalous in some of their lending practices would have enough courage himself to follow through on some of the things he is saying. This goes back to what went on during the period when the bells rang some two weeks ago. We talked about Parliament and the way it was supposed to work. If it is going to work, then it seems to me that the government should be willing to accept amendments that are not all-encompassing. This amendment does not change the intention of the act. The Speaker did not rule this amendment out of order. It is simply there to define further how the act is supposed to work. If we are to have a parliamentary system, it seems to me that there should be no reason why this kind of amendment is not accepted and accepted gladly by the government.
The Minister of Finance says that the banks should bleed a little bit. One of the ways to make the banks bleed a little bit is to have things set up so that we pay a little less interest when borrowing money. When I say "we", I am talking about the farmers. I am a farmer. But what does the government do? It does not want to accept the amendment because it has some hot shot advisers in the department of whom the minister is afraid. We pay their salaries and the minister is responsible for them, but he is afraid to go against their advice. That is some minister of agriculture.
Again, the ultimate in hypocrisy is when the Minister of Finance supports the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Obviously the Minister of Agriculture supports that. But what does he do when it comes time to do something about things? It is easy to say "Phooey on Bouey." Instead of making the banks bleed, we give them a transfusion. But when it comes time to accept a very simple, straightforward amendment in terms of clarifying how a particular section of the act should work, we do not do so.
Very briefly, I find it most unfortunate that I have to rise and use my time this afternoon to point out how inadequate and foolish are some of the statements which the Minister of Agriculture made yesterday when he talked about this very important bill. It is a very important bill, at least it can be in the way farmers are able to finance their operations.
I hope that at third reading I will be able to outline why I think this bill can be very significant in terms of agricultural finance. Let me close simply by saying that I think it most unfortunate that the government did not see fit to accept this simple, straightforward and very helpful amendment. It would have improved the act. If it were an improved act, it would better serve the farming community, and if the community is better served then everyone in this country is better served.
