Mr. Speaker, this is a very important bill with respect to agricultural finance. Perhaps I should qualify that and say it has the potential to become a very important bill. Without being too facetious and without being too disrespectful of the minister, I wonder if he really understands how significant this bill can be. Farmers make up a very small percentage of the population and do not account for very much in terms of political significance or importance. However, they are very important because they produce the most basic commodity of all: food. They have done a very good job of producing high quality food for the Canadian consumer. Not only that, but they have increased production to the extent that agricultural exports account for a significant part of our total exports.
Even though we import a lot of off-season fruits and vegetables, peanuts and other things we cannot grow because of our climate, we still have a significant trade surplus in food. By that I mean that when you add up all of our food exports and subtract our food imports, we still have a significant surplus. The larger the surplus, the easier it is for our dollar and interest rates; the easier it is for interest rates, the better it is for everyone in the country. A lot of people like to buy Japanese cars, and we have a problem in that we have too many of them here. We know that is causing problems for jobs in the automotive industry. However, we are a lot better off trading grain for Japanese cars or cameras than we are simply sending them our dollars. So the production and export of food is very important to this country.
It is also important-I have said this before many times and I like to say it every time I get the chance-because the less money the consumer spends on food, the more he has left over to spend on other things, which by and large means a higher standard of living for the country.
Probably the main reason why agriculture has been so productive is that we have made use of more capital. We now have to invest a tremendous amount of dollars to create a job in agriculture. Recent figures indicate that it takes more
Farm Loans
dollars to create a job in agriculture than it does in most manufacturing industries. That gives an idea of how capitalintensive farmers have become. The more that is so, the more problems we have when interest rates fluctuate. As interest rates go up, the farmer operating on borrowed money has to pay more interest. That causes problems, and that is why this bill is important.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the main reason I think this bill has the potential to be very significant to Canadian agriculture, one which could be used in the small business community because the same principle applies, is because of Section 13, which provides:
The corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means, including issuing and selling bonds, debentures, notes and other evidences of indebtedness of the corporation.
Let me tell the House why that is important. I grew up in the middle of Saskatchewan. I see everyone in the House is overjoyed at that, really sitting on the edge of their chairs!

At any rate, there are some things which need to be said from a western perspective, and I sometimes think we do not say them often enough. We should say them more often, is perhaps a better way of phrasing it. In the early days of western agriculture we had a branch banking system, which still exists. That sytem works in such a way that there is a central bank with several small branches throughout the country. In the early days in Saskatchewan, at least where I grew up, many of those branches were net deposit banks in the fall of the year. By that I mean that when a farmer sold his grain, he put his money in the bank in the fall and the head office of the bank decided where the money would be invested. In almost all cases the money was taken out of the small community and sent to the larger centres to be used to develop areas away from where it was generated.
I can remember my father telling me a story, and I hope he is watching this afternoon. He went into a sub-branch of a branch bank, if you can follow that, Mr. Speaker, and they refused to cash a grain cheque for him. That is how short of cash some of those banks were many years ago. That did nothing to help the immediate area, and that is what has happened in many cases now.
The farmer's pension plan is his land. Economists call this forced savings. Farmers do not have any choice, they do not have a lot of spare cash to spend on recreational activities; they try to pay for their land. They do that because land is very important to people who earn their living from it, and also because it is, in effect, their pension fund. So they are forced to pay for the land. However, when they sell out they take the proceeds and in many cases deposit it in trust accounts, in banks or invest it in stocks and bonds. The situation is still the same in most cases; the money leaves the immediate area of where it was generated. So it is then unavailable to farmers for use in agriculture. This act, however, could mean that they

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
would be able to tap that source of funds. In other words, the money generated from agriculture can stay in the industry to assist younger farmers in becoming established.
There is another reason why 1 think this bill can be very important. Any small business, including a farm, a machinery dealership or any other business run by one man or a family, will try to generate the capital to pay for that business within the lifetime of the operator. In other words, if the farmer wants to own his land, he has to do it in his lifetime. He borrows the money; he pays it back.
That is not the case in terms of larger corporations which can go to the market and issue equity shares. If one buys a share from General Motors, General Motors is not obligated to pay back the value of the share. It is obligated to pay back some kind of dividend on that investment. That simply means that a large corporation is able to obtain equity financing. General Motors, or any of the companies listed on the stock market, is not obligated to repay the value of the share. All it is obligated to pay is some kind of dividend on the share. That is not the case with most small businesses. Any small business must regenerate its capital every time there is a new generation of owners. This is also true with regard to farms. That is why it is once again important that we try to establish some means of keeping the money generated in agriculture working in agriculture.
This bill is very significant, it seems to me, because of Clause 13. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) can make the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) understand my two areas of concern, I am sure the Minister of Finance will agree to go along with some of the suggestions which have been made concerning Clause 13 of this bill.
As I said, this bill is also very important in terms of assisting farmers to finance their operations because of the increased capital farmers need. My guess is that as recently as 20 years ago, a farmer could have taken somewhere between $50,000 and $75,000, and set himself up in a mixed farming operation. Right now, a farmer could easily spend that kind of money on one ordinary tractor, and could spend considerably more than that to purchase a larger four-wheel-drive tractor. Twenty years ago a farm could be completely equipped with the money that one spends today on one tractor. A farmer could have purchased a section of land, livestock and machinery and still have had operating capital left over. That is an indication of the amount of money farmers need today to operate their farms on a yearly basis. It is increasingly important that we recognize the demands farmers are placing on the capital market in order to continue operations.
However, even though all of my dreams would come true in terms of how Clause 13 would work, that is not the total answer as far as farm financing is concerned. Surely the government has an obligation to see that farm incomes at least keep pace with inflation. I believe it was the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) who accurately pointed out that prices of all commodities have drastically dropped over the last couple of years while input costs have risen. Fuel prices have
risen largely because of taxation by the federal government. The costs of fertilizer, repairs and machinery have risen. Interest rates have risen, as have taxes. Virtually every farm operating cost is up, yet the prices of most farm commodities are down. I do not expect there will be any increases in the prices of farm commodities this coming year. The government has a role to play in attempting to see that prices are adequate, because if they are adequate there is less demand for financing. Farmers who earn an adequate income can get by with borrowing less.
There are areas that this government could pursue in connection with the Americans in order to increase prices of feed and cereal grains in world markets. I am not so sure that it is doing enough in that respect. There has been a great deal of comment recently to the effect that the federal government has been reneging on its responsibility toward a nationally coordinated and at least partially funded stabilization program for both beef and hogs, yet we see nothing on the horizon in this context. I wish there were some evidence of leadership, genuine interest and care. I am sure there are some avenues that the federal government and the Minister of Agriculture could pursue to ensure that the members of the farming community receive better incomes, and then the necessity for borrowing would be less.
The capital gains issue is another problem for farmers. If there were a different system of capital gains where a farmer paid less in capital gains when he disposed of his farm after working for many years to pay for it, the need for farm financing would also be less. Some people simply ask, "Well, why would that be?" That is because a farmer considers his piece of land to be his retirement fund. He pays for it over his productive lifetime. He decides how much money he will need to live on for the rest of his life. That is one of the determining factors in the price he asks for his land. However, if he must deduct a big chunk of capital gains tax from that price, then he must ask for more money for his land. That drives up the price of land, and that is what is happening. Therefore, if we had a more sensible approach to capital gains, the need for farm financing would considerably decrease.
1 do not think I need relate the problems the last budget has caused by the removal of the IAAC provisions and their replacement with forward averaging. That is really a system whereby the federal government has a bigger tax grab on income farmers and businessmen derive from the sale of capital assets upon retirement or at any other time when capital assets are sold.
Again referring back to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), it is clearly evident that the small business bond concept introduced in the November 12 budget is just not working. In fact, I do not know of one small business bond which has been granted since November 12. I do not understand why the government does not admit that this type of bond is not working. We must at least give the government credit for caring or seeing the situation clearly enough to realize that
March 30, 1982

there is a need, and for attempting to address it with a small business bond. However, it should now be evident to the government, approximately four months after the introduction of the budget, that the small business bond concept is not working and that prior to the budget the Small Business Development Bond concept was working. I believe many people who are knowledgeable in this area would agree that if the government is serious about meeting that need, it should return to the provisions of the Small Business Development Bond. That would make a lot of sense to a lot of people.
I do not believe farm financing should be considered to be the total solution to any of the problems. In fact, the real solution is to do something about farm income so that farmers will be in a position to generate as much of their capital requirements as possible from their own operations without having to go to the government or to the banks. I hope this bill will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to begin expanding its loans so that it can meet the needs of a higher percentage of farmers who have come to rely upon it.
The first loan I ever took out was a Farm Credit Corporation loan. I remember it well. In fact, I still have the piece of equipment I bought with that original loan. Your Honour is nodding. You must think I am pretty old and that it must have been a good piece of equipment. It was a good piece of equipment. It just goes to show that the Farm Credit Corporation has well served many people in this country. However, in the last number of years it has been unable to meet the need because it has been strapped for funds. Therefore, if this bill allows, the Farm Credit Corporation to go to the market to obtain additional funds, the corporation will be back in the position where it can once again meet the needs of the farming community.
I would like to stress that it would be helpful if farmers were given an opportunity to lend money through a small business bond, an agribond or some other concept which could come into play as a result of this bill. If farmers were given a chance to lend money to the Farm Credit Corporation, I believe many would choose to do so, even at a lower interest rate. I believe many farmers would be willing to accept somewhat less of a return on their money if they knew that it was staying in their own communities to help young farmers. Presently they are not getting that opportunity. We really will not know whether my thinking and my suggestion on this matter is correct until it is tried.
Let me give an example. Many people who grow up in a community have a sense of identity with that community. They have lived there for 30, 40 or 50 years, they choose to retire and they feel that they have been well served by their community. They would like to put something back into that area. If they are given an opportunity, through some kind of an agribond concept that would bear less interest, they would be willing to accept that if they knew that the money they were lending to the Farm Credit Corporation was going to help their community.

I could give many examples showing how that system has worked across the United States, where they have a unit banking system. Banks there are owned, by and large, in small communities in the same way as a grocery store. The first line of thinking of any of those local banks is that their community should survive, since that in itself means the survival of the community. We could make use some of the pride that individuals have in their communities, in agriculture, in small towns, if we would offer agribonds at a lower rate of interest, provided the people offering that money to the Farm Credit Corporation know where that money is going.
I could touch on many other areas of farm financing. As I have said, this can be a significant bill. The Minister of Agriculture will get my support and the support of my colleagues if he attempts to get the Minister of Finance to let the Farm Credit Corporation borrow money, by any means, in order that that corporation may be in a better position to fulfil its mandate of providing adequate financing for the farmers. If we can do that we will be serving the farming community, we will serve the consumers and also serve the whole country.
Again, I have to congratulate the minister for this bill, or at least for this one clause, because it can be a very significant bill as a result of the inclusion of Section 13.

When I spoke on this bill at second reading, Mr. Speaker, I noted that there were a couple of difficulties which would need to be addressed at the committee stage. For example, I was told a year ago by Farm Credit Corporation officials that they would like to see a clear legislative guideline allowing them to treat a farmer's spouse as an equal partner, so that in a case where both the husband and the wife run and operate a farm, each would qualify for farm credit funding.
The present bill contains no such spelled-out provision, so 1 raised the matter in committee again. The matter has been discussed and the Farm Credit Corporation was given a clear indication that both spouses actively engaged in farming could receive farm credit funding.
I suppose they will run into the difficulty of a farm wife who has a job as a schoolteacher or who works in the nursing profession or is doing some office work, but we would certainly expect to see her taking her place beside her spouse operating that farm actively and helping in its operation, and that should be recognized as a partnership and should qualify for that type of funding.
I accept these assurances from the Farm Credit Corporation, but I know that other members also will want to monitor the situation as time passes to ensure that the policy works in practice. Otherwise we shall know that we need to give legislative expression to the equality between men and women which we on all sides of the House recognize as essential to the Constitution of our country.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) appears to believe that no legislative mechanism needs to be provided to

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
ensure fair treatment for partners who happen also to be married. I for one am going to give the minister the opportunity to prove himself right, now that his officials have indicated the intention to deal equitably with spouses in this regard,
On second reading also I noted that while we were increasing the potential of farm credit lending by $1,875 billion, we were not automatically ensuring that the corporation would have access to the funds, allowing the lending of anything like that amount. Each year the corporation receives only a fraction of its authorized capital and is accordingly enabled to borrow 25 times that capital addition. We in this party have been arguing that the Farm Credit Corporation has been given too little funding for some years back to allow it to meet the needs of agriculture.
The present bill giving the Farm Credit Corporation access to privately borrowed funds should provide the flexibility to permit the annual authorization of capital to match the perceived need for funding for land acquisition. Treasury Board should no longer need to keep its eyes so much on the need to lend the Farm Credit Corporation 25 times the amount of capital it authorizes each year, since a part of what the corporation borrows can now come from sources other than the Consolidated Revenue Fund. For this reason, the bill is an improvement on the present situation. Yet it is worth noting that during the period since the present minister first took charge of the agriculture portfolio, the percentage of long-term credit provided to agriculture by the Farm Credit Corporation has fallen from some 70 per cent to a mere 25 per cent. In other words, there has been a very significant erosion of the Farm Credit Corporation's role.
It is no use blaming the banks for the failure to keep the corporation supplied with funds. This legislation is overdue as a means of ensuring that the farmers are not forced into the hands of the banks for land purchases. We will have to ensure that the corporation is enabled by this bill to move back in the direction of a greater rate of participation in farm financing.
Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that farmers are not to blame for the high cost of land or for the ridiculously high cost of financing high-cost land. This is the fault of a high-spending government with too little concern for the role of investment in creating wealth, one that is responsible for putting us as a country in the position of having to pay unsupportable costs for investment in land or in any other kind of capital business plant. This bill helps to repair the damage caused farmers by government policies over some years that have made land very high in price and land financing next to impossible.
This leads me to a point I wish to emphasize strongly, Mr. Speaker. In my part of Ontario we have reached the point where the high cost of land and land financing is leading to a steady erosion of Canadian ownership of Canada's farm land. Among those who have stayed on the land, while many of their fellows have moved into our cities, there is a very strong commitment to retain the tradition of family-owned and operated farms. Canadians as a whole benefit enormously from the commitment of these people to a life of hard work, to
tremendous productivity, and to producing very high quality and inexpensive food.
The measure of the success of our farmers is that Canadians take their farming industry almost for granted. Indeed, Canadian farming is so efficient and productive that it could almost be taken for granted, if it were not for the tremendous burdens imposed on farmers in financing their operations.
It is so much in the interests of Canada to ensure that family farms survive, and that this pool of dedicated and productive talent is not dissipated, that we should make every effort possible to ensure that public policy does not undermine the family farm. And yet, that is what the policy of high interest rates is doing. In the past two years, when even the best and most well-established farmers have lost a good deal of the equity they had built up in their operations over a lifetime, our farmers have, in effect, been subsidizing the consumer.
It could be argued that farmers have to compete for a market like other businessmen, and most farmers do not object to the principle of a competitive market for many of their products. My point is that farmers are willing to compete to sell their product to the Canadian consumer, but the high cost of financing their operations reduces their capacity to compete.
It is not inefficiency in their production but inefficiency in this government's policy that has pushed farmers into the position of seeing their investment erode. For many of them, this erosion to date has simply meant that they own less of their operation than they did two years ago. For an increasing number, however, it means that they no longer own anything. The alarming bankruptcy figures are only the tip of the iceberg. Many who have not gone bankrupt have been forced to sell out just short of bankruptcy; otherwise, the bankruptcy figures would be far worse. Even as they are, the bankruptcy figures are a national shame and disgrace. They are evidence of a bankruptcy of policy, a bankruptcy that is made doubly evident by the attempt of last November's budget to take away the retirement funds which many of our farmers have been building toward, throughout their working careers, by scrimping, saving, making do with small disposable incomes so that they would have capital with which to retire. They do not have indexed pensions. Most of them do not even own a home when they leave the farm. All their retirement needs must be supplied from the sale of their farming operation. The government has shown its insensitivity toward this fact by regarding farmers as though they were profiteers.
As for young farmers, those who must supply the next generation of food producers, the government's policy has made it more and more difficult for the young to enter a farming career. Land costs are very high. I do not for a moment suggest that this government is solely responsible for the increase in the value of land during the past decade or more, but if land costs reflect the value of land directly, they are high because there is a high market value for land.
March 30, 1982

Given the demonstrated capacity of our farmers to use land efficiently, young or beginning farmers do not so much regret the high value of the land they wish to purchase, but they regret the high financing costs. Farm credit helps in many cases to make the difference between allowing a young farmer to make a career in farming or not. That is why this bill is a valuable piece of legislation in so far as it will make that difference, I hope, to a great many young farmers.
As I say, for two years there has been a growing apprehension in my part of Canada that our farm financing policy is not working well enough. Foreign ownership of our land has become more than a threat. It is an alarming and growing reality. In the community I represent, and very close to my own home, there are numbers of farms that have been bought by numbered companies. Certainly we are very suspicious that those numbered companies have been established for the sole purpose of buying agricultural land, particularly in the area that I represent. We know that is a fact that we can substantiate. It is becoming more evident all the time.
The reasons are not hard to see. Our young potential farmers have to borrow to buy land. They have to borrow at upwards of 16 per cent and often at a great deal more than that. Foreign capital looking for a safe haven is attracted to Canada's farm land for two reasons. One is that investment in land in a country with a peaceful constitutional history is a safe place to store wealth. Another is that our farm land is still a relatively good value compared to land in many European countries where urban sprawl has eaten up a good deal of the available land and where the demand for food by consumers is high because of the dense urban population.
What makes the purchase of our farm land particularly attractive to foreigners is that the high cost of farm financing here inevitably has a depressive effect upon the demand for land by Canadian purchasers. In Germany, for example, mortgage rates for house purchases are low, presently no more than about 10 per cent. Since there are no exchange controls preventing a German house owner from mortgaging his house and investing the proceeds here, it is clear that a German investor of ordinary means can compete for Canadian farm land at a rate of interest well below anything a young Canadian farmer could hope to get. I say this not by any means to criticize the German policy by which such low interest rates are maintained, but rather to point out at what a disadvantage our high interest rates place Canadians who wish to buy and farm our land.
What is true in the case of Germany is true in the case of other European countries as well. Perhaps the only thing that has kept back an even greater flood of foreign investment capital to buy our available land is that many foreigners have too little confidence in the ability of this government to maintain the value of our currency, to feel secure in investing here.
Paradoxically, then, we are vulnerable to foreign speculation in our land, but protected from even greater vulnerability by the perceived economic incompetence of this government. This is poor comfort to our young farmers.
Farm Loans
To put this problem of increasing foreign purchases of our land in perspective, let me mention the situation in a township which I know very well. In that township during the past year, foreign land ownership, according to reliable figures prepared by the Federation of Agriculture, have increased from 320 acres to more than 2,300 acres. In the adjoining township it has gone from zero to 1,100 acres. I think the latest statistics would even show an increase from that.
A little farther north in Bruce County, near the growing community that surrounds the Bruce nuclear power development, recent figures have shown that 2,000 acres in a single part of one township have recently been purchased by foreign investors. No one can blame farmers who sell to foreign investors. They are the customers who are able to meet the costs of the purchase. No one can blame young Canadian farmers either for not meeting the price; they are caught by the high interest rate policy of the government.
The vast majority of those who have land to sell would like to see their land pass into the hands of owners who live on the land and farm it. They do not care whether the owner is Canadian-born or a recent immigrant who intends to farm it and live on it; what they do care about is seeing the family farm survive. Heaven knows, we are all immigrants if we go back just a few generations. What farmers in this part of Canada, and I suspect elsewhere throughout Canada, do not want to see is absentee ownership. Neither do the municipal governments in the rural areas want to see an erosion of the social character of their township.
We found many townships and communities that had greater amounts of foreign ownership dominating those areas. Often the new buyers come in and remove the existing buildings, which results in a lower assessment value. There is not as good a tax structure base. There is also a problem when putting in field tile in municipal ditches, which we have to do in that part of Ontario. It is often difficult to find the proper owner to get permission. Co-operation has always existed in the communities throughout Ontario, and I am sure throughout Canada where the farmers have worked together. All of a sudden there are new problems to face. Everyone worked on line fences or property fences. This is something that is disappearing. We have had many families living on the farms helping to shape the local society ever since the land was settled. We hate to see that disappear as well.
Because this problem of foreign ownership has sprung up only within the past two or three years, it is apparent that the policy of high interest rates and inadequate funding for the Farm Credit Corporation is involved. It may well be that we should be looking now, not when the dikes have burst, at the radically harmful social and economic effects to Canada of a policy that allows our excellent and highly developed farm land to pass into foreign hands while the generation of Canadians who would become our food producers and would maintain a competitive efficiency we have come to take for granted are driven away from agriculture.
I should also mention that in some of our deliberations in committee I raised the matter of transferring existing farm

Farm Loans
credit mortgages. Section 16(f) of the act states that the mortgage given to secure the loan shall contain a covenant by the borrower that he will not use the proceeds for any purposes except those approved by the act, and that he will not dispose of the property without the consent of the corporation.
Clause 11(4) of Bill C-88 states that if the borrower sells the land without FCC permission, the loan becomes due immediately. This clause may make it easier for the Farm Credit Corporation to refuse to allow farm takeovers by foreigners, but it does not prohibit them from allowing foreigners to take over the existing Farm Credit Corporation mortgages. That is solely at the discretion of the Farm Credit Corporation. 1 would have felt more comfortable if it had been written into the act that the legislation would disallow the transfer of that mortgage. It is something we have to watch closely and give support to Farm Credit Corporation officials in cases of transfers of mortgages such as that. We in Parliament should labour to ensure that it never becomes the norm of Canadian agriculture, because if it does, our days of cheap, domestically-produced food are gone forever.
In saying that, I support this present bill. I want to note that the bill arrives on a scene that is rapidly changing. We can be glad that the Farm Credit Corporation is able to do the job it does, and we hope it will recover some of the ground it has lost through the underfunding to which I referred earlier.
But already, as we pass this bill into law, it is apparent that we have not solved the embarrassing problem of farm financing. A warning is being sounded daily by our farmers that we are not doing enough to ensure the continuance of the family farm in Canada and that we are permitting this most vital of all sectors to fall into the hands of those who do not have the same vital interest in feeding Canadians efficiently and cheaply as do those Canadians living on the land. It is not just young farmers who want to buy land who are sounding this warning. It is also being sounded by retiring farmers who are ready to sell their land, as well as municipal councillors who are watchful of the social character of the communities they serve. In accepting the present bill we should listen to the warning they are giving and recognize that the bill has not made us secure in the agricultural sector, but has merely made us less insecure.
The means of producing our food should never pass from the hands of Canadians into the hands of foreigners, or even of absentee owners. If this happened, there could come a day when it would be more expedient for foreign owners to withdraw our land from production than to keep it in production. Erosion of the family farm is an invitation to further land exchanges which lead to corporate farming. These are matters Parliament should address.
In welcoming this bill, as far as it goes, I look forward to seeing legislation along the lines we have suggested earlier, which even the Minister of Agriculture seemed to regard with approval when he said, earlier in debate, that in the future consideration could be given to providing special tax concessions on bonds sold by the Farm Credit Corporation or on
registered retirement saving funds placed with the corporation by retiring farmers.
We are in agreement, then, that what we have here is welcome legislation, but it is not enough. Let us hope that while the Farm Credit Corporation makes good use of the provisions in this bill, for the sake of Canadian agriculture the minister will concern himself with preparing further measures to ensure that agriculture for which he has responsibility remains Canadian agriculture.
In conclusion, I would just like to add that this bill is something long overdue. Agriculture needs this measure very badly. I have said before that agriculture needs the proper tools with which to work. Financing is one of those tools. Financing is like farm equipment. It does not matter what part of the country; we know that if machinery is not kept up to date, crops cannot be grown. I strongly believe that farm credit can and will be an important tool. We look forward to seeing this legislation in place very quickly and working for farmers.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in the debate today and to associate myself with the comments of my colleagues who have spoken earlier in the debate. Clearly, the legislation we are dealing with today will be of benefit to Canadian farmers. It is not our intention to delay passage of the bill, but I think it is important that we put some remarks on the record with regard to the crisis in Canadian agriculture today, and with regard to the fact that this bill and other measures which have been proposed by the government will not do enough to deal with the urgent situation confronting Canadian farmers.
As someone keenly interested in the problems of Canadian farmers, Mr. Speaker, I know you will appreciate the fact that a story that is told in my neck of the woods perhaps describes the situation of Canadian farmers today as graphically as anything else I could tell the House. They tell a story about two farmers in my constituency who live near each other. They bought tickets on a lottery and were hoping that one of them would have the good fortune to win a million dollars. One farmer turned to his neighbour and asked: "If you win the million dollars on the lottery, how do you intend to spend it? What will you do with it?" His neighbour's comment was: "Well, what I would do is sell my farm and move to Florida. I would put all the money in the bank and simply live on the interest and have happy days for the rest of my life." He turned to his friend and said, "Now, if you win the million dollars, what would you do?" His friend said: "Well, I kind of like farming. I think I would stay in farming until the million was gone." I do not think there is any more accurate way of describing the plight of Canadian farmers today than to repeat that story because notwithstanding repeated commitments by the government, and particularly by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), record numbers of Canadian farmers are being driven off the land.
Bill C-88 before us today will be helpful in terms of increasing the amount of capital available to Canadian farmers.
March 30, 1982

There is no opposition on this side of the House to the bill. It is a bill that we believe is necessary and should have been passed long ago. Indeed, the bill was in the works during the time of the Clark government, and the real question is why it has taken the Minister of Agriculture so long. He was restored to his office as Minister of Agriculture over two years ago, and the question Canadian farmers should be asking him is why he has been so slow in taking the step he is taking in the House today.
The most important element of the bill is that it would enable the Farm Credit Corporation to go outside the Consolidated Revenue Fund-outside the government-and seek funds in the private market in the hope of raising enough capital to enable it to lend money to a larger number of Canadian farmers.
No doubt the most critical issue facing Canadian agriculture today is the question of low returns for farmers and ever-escalating prices as they attempt to do their job. Certainly the most important component of those ever-increasing costs is the cost of financing. I do not think anyone who has attended a meeting of his local federation of agriculture or of any commodity group would be unaware of the fact that farmers in all parts of the country find themselves in a very serious cash bind. They find that even if they are capable of getting loans from their local banks or from some government agency, it is very difficult, no matter what commodity a farmer is in today, to even be able to pay the carrying charges on loans. This is why it is essential that instead of simply applying band aids to the problems facing Canadian farmers, the Minister of Agriculture should be interceding with his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), to address the critical problem of interest rates in Canada.
What has been done by this government since the election in 1980 to bring down interest rates? What we have seen, what Canadian farmers have seen, what business people have seen and what home owners have seen is successive increases in interest rates and very little action taken by the government to insulate the weakest and poorest members of our society from the tremendous burden which has been inflicted on them by the government. This is why it is essential that the Minister of Agriculture, if he is to do his duty on behalf of Canadian farmers from one coast to the other, stops simply talking about the banks, trying to shift the blame on them and trying to blame other people for the government's high interest rate policy and, instead, deals directly with the Minister of Finance and insists that the Minister of Finance change policies which have been disastrous for Canadian farmers, just as they have been disastrous for home owners and small business people in this country. Until the government is prepared to come to grips with the consequences of its economic scorched-earth policies which are putting such an unfair burden on ordinary Canadians, there is no way this measure or other measures currently before the House will ensure that Canadian agriculture remains viable for the future.
The simple fact is that the true minister of agriculture in Canada is not the gentleman who often wears a green hat and who attends meetings of federations of agriculture around the
Farm Loans
country. The true minister of agriculture in Canada today is the Minister of Finance. He is the one who decides what the policies are which will directly affect Canadian farmers. He is the one who decides how much money will be allocated to the Farm Credit Corporation as authorized lending capital. He is the one who is responsible for interest rates in Canada. He is the one who makes decisions which affect the day to day lives of Canadian farmers, just as he is the one whose decisions affect the day to day lives of other Canadians in other sectors. I think Canadian farmers are beginning to weary of hearing the Minister of Agriculture attempt to shift the blame. The fact is that he is part of a cabinet which has consciously adopted a policy of high interest rates and is consciously attempting, by putting a burden on ordinary Canadians, to squeeze them very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, I noticed you did not rule on whether that is a point of order. Clearly it is not, but I am delighted to respond to my colleague's question because there is a number of things which could be done by the government. No effort has been made by the government, particularly during the big-spending sixties and seventies, to control the federal deficit. A major component in the inflation we have today is a direct result of this government's high spending programs. If, as the Minister of Finance says, the reason for high interest rates today is that inflation is running at a record level-and it is, as a result of the minister's policies-then the most significant thing the government could have done was to get some control of its spending and bring the deficit under control. Instead, it has moved consistently in the other direction.
It was the Progressive Conservative government that proposed the concept of the small business development bond which was designed to give some relief to Canadian farmers and small business people so they would have a buffer to ease the burden of high interest rates. In the budget of the Minister of Finance, brought down the day after Remembrance Day last November, we find that he is actually counting on the fact that the Small Business Development Bond will cost the Canadian government less money this year than last year. In other words, the terms for lending are more restrictive this year than they were last year. An applicant will have to demonstrate that he is virtually insolvent before he is eligible for financing under the program. I will admit that the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance and their Liberal colleagues are doing everything they can to ensure that small business people and farmers are virtually insolvent. But that is not the way to deal with their problems, Mr. Speaker.
I have illustrated two ways in which the government could have acted, Mr. Speaker. Unless it is prepared to come to grips

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
with the whole question of the government deficit and inflation, which is caused by federal government spending, there is no way that adequate relief will be found for farmers, particularly with the palliatives that have been put before parliament today. Bill C-88 will not provide the required relief. I suggest that no member on the government side could in honesty claim that this bill will bring an end to farm bankruptcies.
Last year alone there were 261 farm bankruptcies in the country, 140 of them in the province of Ontario. Anyone who has had the opportunity of meeting with farmers in any part of the country knows that under the tenure of the government, since the last election, the problems facing them have become more and more acute. The threats of bankruptcies have increased dramatically. The problems that young farmers face who are trying to get into farming and continue with the family farm, become more and more insurmountable as each day passes.
For the government to try to shift the blame to someone else by saying that it is held hostage to international events and that it has nothing to do with the inflation rate in Canada which is higher than that in the United States, or that it has nothing to do with the interest rates it is directly responsible for, is doing a disservice to Canadians.
If we are to attack the economic problems facing farmers or any other Canadian, the first thing we must do is deal honestly with the situation and admit that the federal government's policies have been wrong-headed. A policy designed to reduce inflation by jacking up interest rates, is contradictory.
When the cost of inventory for a business increases, do we seriously, expect that business to sell its goods for less this year than it did last year? Naturally, whenever possible, it will attempt to increase the selling price in order to cover cost. And if the costs to working people increase, do we expect unions to settle for less money next year than they do this year? Clearly the incentive will be for them to increase their demands.
Far from being a cure for inflation in Canada today, high interest rates are a serious contributing factor and are a tremendous burden on ordinary Canadians.
On February 23, 1982, the Kitchener-Waterloo Record ran an article on the front page with the heading "Whelan vows $1 billion in aid-" This occurred at the closed meeting with Canadian farmers. The second paragraph of the article reads as follows:
But Whelan reportedly also told the farm leaders that if they quoted him to the press, he will deny it.
Indeed he has, Mr. Speaker. It is not good enough for the Minister of Agriculture to go around the country saying one thing to farmers and then come back here and support the government's high interest rate policies. It is not good enough for him to continue to tell one story to Canadian farmers and support policies which have been very damaging to farmers and which affect their ability to stay in business.
When my friend across the way bootlegged in a question under the guise of a point of order he asked me what could be done by the government or if anything could be done to
provide relief to Canadian farmers. I have mentioned one thing, Mr. Speaker. We have to get inflation under control. Interest rates must be brought down. The government washes its hands of responsibility but it is directly reponsible, Mr. Speaker, and must be held accountable for the consequences of its policies.
There is the matter of the small business bond. The government policies in this respect are far too restrictive. Each member can ask how many farmers he knows who have been able to qualify for the bond or how many small businessmen have been able to qualify for it this year. The government is tightening up on eligibility. People now have to carry a much heavier burden and they are doing so without the assistance they so desperately need.
Another element of the budget which is obviously affecting farmers is the IAAC, the Income Averaging Annuity Contract. For the family farmer, his pension is in the land. But the Minister of Finance abolished the IAAC provision for some unspecified income-averaging provision which has still to be spelled out. There are serious doubts about the tax treatment of the farmer who is forced to sell the family farm.
There is the matter of capital gains tax on the family farm. In its budget the Progressive Conservative government provided for capital gains tax relief for family farmers. What happened to that since the 1980 election? Have members of the Liberal caucus tried to stress to the Minister of Finance- the real minister of agriculture today-that it is time some relief was given to bona fide family farmers?
All Canadians are desperately affected by the health and vitality of Canadian agriculture, Mr. Speaker. I cannot walk through any community in my constituency without recognizing that when farmers are doing well, people in the towns are also doing well. If we are serious about redressing our trade imbalance, if we are serious about ensuring that we are not held hostage in the future with food the way we have been with oil in the past, then it is essential that the family farm be kept alive. To do that we must ensure fair prices for the farmer. We must ensure that the price he has to pay for goods and services needed to conduct his business, is fair. We have to ensure that interest rates do not become a crushing burden which makes it impossible for him to carry on. We must provide incentives to the Canadian family farmer to keep him on the land and for young farmers to come back to the business and remain in it.
There seems to be a philosophy within the Department of Finance that all they need to do in times of high inflation is to turn the screws on ordinary Canadians-to slow down the economy, put a few thousand people out of jobs, and that as time improves they can turn the screw the other way. People will then be happy, businesses will be open, productivity will increase and we will be back where we were before. That simply is not the case, Mr. Speaker.
If a family farmer of 45 years of age who has experience in farming, knows his business and is at the peak of his productivity, is forced off the land today and into the city to seek a job, does the government really seriously believe that even if
March 30, 1982

the economy recovers within two or three years, he is going to move back to the farm and start all over again? Surely anyone concerned with the problems facing agriculture today must admit that the philosophy that seems to be present in the Department of Finance is not very sound in reality. It would be helpful if the bureaucrats who devise the policies that farmers have to live with could spend some time in rural Canada and have the opportunity to talk to people there about the effect of those policies. Ordinary Canadians are suffering at the hands of people who simply do not understand their problems or are indifferent to the consequences of the policies they promote.
We support this measure, Mr. Speaker, because any relief for Canadian farmers and anything that can be done to increase the amount of capital available from the Farm Credit Corporation, is a positive move. But let us not kid ourselves. This measure is only a first step. It will help to relieve some of the burden created by government policy, but it does not address the root cause of the problems. Until the Minister of Finance is prepared to recognize that the policies he has been following have been dangerous to ordinary Canadians, until he is prepared to change those policies and to provide some relief for ordinary people who are carrying a burden too heavy for many of them to bear, these problems will continue for farmers and for people in other areas.
I call upon the Minister of Agriculture to do his duty on behalf of Canadian farmers by going to the Minister of Finance and saying that it is time for those policies to be changed. If he would do that, the Minister of Agriculture would serve Canadian farmers better than anything else he has done to date.

Mr. Speaker, at the six o'clock adjournment I had just started to speak about capital gains taxes as they affect our farmers. In my view, capital gains tax is very unfair. A farmer or a businessman whose only pension is his land or his business, pays taxes on his land or his business all his life. When a farmer or a businessman reaches retirement age and wants to use his pension-his land or business which is his nest egg-what does the government do? It takes another chunk of it in capital gains tax. This form of taxation is one of the grievances that many farmers have. Farmers are not in favour of capital gains taxes. The capital gains taxes that are levied now by government are more unfair than they have been for a number of years. When a farmer comes to receive his pension-his land-often he is only able to sell it on the instalment plan no matter whether he sells his farm to a son, to a daughter, or to someone outside the family. Seldom can a farmer sell a family farm to a large corporation, and farmers do not want to do this because they want to retain their family farms. Consequently, most often a farmer has to sell his farm on the instalment plan.
Take for instance a farm that has been brought up to a value of $200,000. Selling that farm on an instalment plan means that the farmer accepts a very small amount of that sum over a period of years. Perhaps he is given a down payment of $10,000 but the original budget said he would have to pay capital gains tax on the full $200,000. That is a most unfair proposition. After some discussion and representations against this proposition, the minister told us in December that if the farm was being sold to the farmer's family the payments could be spread over ten years, but if the farm was sold to an outsider, the payments would be spread over five years. But the plan is still most unfair. It takes the pension right out of the
farmer's pocket. That was the pension he built up in order to have a decent standard of living for the rest of his life and to have enough money to look after his family. Instead, what we are doing is saying to the farmer, "You have been working building up a nest egg but now the government will grab up a chunk of it." That means that many of our farmers have been unable to complete the deal they started prior to November 12. They cannot live on the balance that would be left. Would any hon. member here upon retirement like it if the government suddenly were to tax a big chunk of his or her pension? If that were done it would put many people in this House in a precarious financial position.
But how much more does this measure affect our farmers and our businessmen whose only pension and only hope of retirement is his land or business? I suggest that we do unto others as we would like others do unto us. We are not doing that in this bill. Our farmers are agonizing over this situation and are being aggravated by it. I have received letters expressing this agony and letters that would make you cry. Farmers are saying that this budget has ruined their hopes. The things they have worked for for 50 years have now gone down the drain. Their wives and family are going to suffer as well as themselves. Others have said: now I cannot sell my land, or expand my business, because of these capital gains taxes. But this government still clings to capital gains tax. Not only that, it has even done away with the once in a lifetime exemption. The government wants every cent it can get, regardless of whether that drives our farmers and businessmen to the poorhouse. It is not fair, and I tell the people it is not fair. The people across this country will support the fact that the farmer's pension is his land. We are now digging into those pensions and interfering with their retirement.
The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Tousignant) asked the minister before the adjournment how he would lower interest rates. Well, I do not think it is so difficult. We now have an interest rate of 16.75 per cent. That is better than 24 per cent or 25 per cent, certainly, but it is still too high. I want to suggest that the practice of the Farm Credit Corporation making money on farm loans is not fair. When you make a loan to a business, it adds the cost to its product and the consumer pays. When you make a loan to a farmer, the farmer cannot add the cost to his product. It has to come out of his margin of profit and that margin is sometimes pretty low or non-existent. That is why there has been so many farm bankruptcies. We keep taking and taking from the farmer and it is getting to the point where there is just nothing left. He cannot pass these costs on like other people and for that reason the government would be justified in having a different policy on loans to farmers.

Mr. Speaker, I usually say it is a pleasure for me to speak on any particular bill in this House. However, when it comes to a bill such as Bill C-88, which deals with loans to farmers, I cannot honestly say it is a pleasure, because what we are really referring to in this bill is a pretty sad story right across our country. It refers to a virtually neglected group within our society. I am not saying that in any cheap way to gain sympathy outside this chamber or among the farmers in my constituency.
I can recall when I first moved to Brant county in 1959 that there were approximately 2,300 farmers. Today we have about 800. Admittedly, back in the 1960s there were some farmers who either did not have the gumption or the intelligence, perhaps, or the will, or the money, or the inclination to hang in, hold on, expand, modernize and so on in order to keep up with changing conditions. Therefore, it was natural that some would fall by the wayside. It was natural that some would give up in the early sixties and the mid-sixties. It was natural that some farmers' sons and daughters would move off the farms. When there is such a reduction in the total number of farmers in one relatively small but very rich farming area of southern Ontario, a reduction from 2,300 to approximately 800 farmers, it obviously must mean something other than just a lack of will or determination.
Farm Loans
When we speak about Bill C-88, we are speaking about the plight of many farmers today. In effect, the only problem facing them today is the problem of financing their operation because of the lack of sufficient cash flow.
There is an even worse situation or even worse problem today when it is virtually impossible for many farmers to get credit at all. They simply cannot afford to borrow any more. The cash flow, in other words, has become virtually a trickle and in many cases has dried up.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we have a situation in which their operating costs are soaring, due to increased energy costs, such as gasoline and diesel fuel, heating costs, drying costs, the cost of fertilizer, and the rising cost of farm machinery. They cannot borrow money; they cannot afford the carrying charges.
Because they cannot afford farm machinery, this is having a very serious adverse effect on the agricultural implement industry, whose Canadian centre, one might say, is also in my constituency in the city of Brantford. Massey-Ferguson and White Farm are both experiencing difficulty in selling their products. The reason they cannot sell combines, at $ 120,000 or $130,000, is that farmers cannot afford to buy on borrowed money. That is another major problem.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, beef producers, hog producers, and cash croppers specifically, are all in trouble. Commodity prices are lower than they were two years ago. All of this is adding to their woes. Then we have Bill C-88 which is a bill to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to seek funding from sources in addition to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. I would not care, if this bill gave the Farm Credit Corporation the right to allow the corporation to use funds from every financial institution in the country-$100 million, $500 million, $1 billion, it makes no difference-the problem is that farmers cannot afford 16.75 per cent interest. Many farmers have had to borrow from banks at higher interest rates than that.
So we get back to the budget, we get back to the No. 1 problem of this country, high interest rates. You can put $100 million, $500 million or $1 billion into the fund, but as long as you are artificially forcing these rates higher and higher- 16.75 per cent is about as high as farm credit has been, I believe, and it may go even higher-it is not going to help the farmer who is carrying charges or a debt load on an annual basis in my constituency that may go as high as $50,000 or $60,000 just to pay interest on money borrowed.
Last summer I visited several farmers, most of them young farmers, who back in the 1970s had been encouraged by both government and the banks to go out and borrow, borrow, borrow in order to expand and modernize. I suppose it makes sense. In order to keep up with technological change in the farming industry, farmers had to spend more money and to spend more money they had to borrow. The banks were throwing it at them. Banks managers never went near the farm, never did profit appraisals. They said: "Here is the money at 8 per cent or 9 per cent, take $200,000, take

$300,000." Now, of course, with the interest rates the banks are charging, from 17 per cent to 19 per cent, the farmers, most of whom are young, ambitious and aggressive, are being forced out of business or forced into a nervous breakdown or a severe depression because they cannot see their way out of this tunnel.
One farmer not far from my city of Brantford told me that the Farm Credit Corporation officer told him: "Look, you have two farms, put the two together and sell them, they are worth about $1.2 million." The farmer said: "Fine, you get me a buyer and I will sell tomorrow." Who can buy a $1.2 million farm operation if, in addition to the amount of the market value of the farm, you are borrowing money at 16 per cent to 18 per cent interest?
Here we are, Mr. Speaker, in a very real dilemma. It does not matter how much money the Farm Credit Corporation can provide, if the interest rates are maintained at a very high level, farmers will not derive any benefit at all. They may keep the wolf from the door for a few more months, they may keep the bailiff away for a few more months, but in the long run the farmers are going deeper and deeper into debt.
Let us look at some of these statistics, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the financial crunch that farmers find themselves in. One could argue that most small businesses today are in trouble; but let us face it, the farmer cannot pass on those added costs as can most other businesses. Most farmers today operate under marketing boards and marketing agencies where prices are pretty well set well ahead, and it is pretty difficult to tack on the added costs of either a mortgage or simply a bank loan for machinery.
Let us look at some of the farm net incomes. In 1973 net farm income was $3.3 billion. In 1980 it was $3.25 billion but in 1973 dollars that was approximately $1.74 billion. In 1981 it was $4 billion net farm income. In 1982 the estimated farm income is going to drop to $3.4 billion. If we read that figure in terms of 1973 dollars the net farm income will be $3.3 billion. We had net farm income, taking into consideration the inflationary figure, of $1.45 billion in 1981. That is a pretty bad picture for the farm industry. The average farm income in 1973 was $12,692 per farm. In 1980, if we look at it in terms of 1973 figures, we get an average or net income per farm of $5,576 in 1973 dollars.
I do not know of any other industry in this country, Mr. Speaker, that is getting so far behind. On the one hand you have very high interest rates; then in the centre you have falling prices in beef, in hogs, in commodities, in most grains, and on the other hand, you have inflation eating away at what income a farmer can get. So, in an inflationary sense, you had an average farm income in 1980 of $5,576 per farm in terms of 1973 dollars.
I do not know how much longer the good farmers of this country, the aggressive farmers, the productive farmers, can tolerate this kind of adversity on a day to day basis. Farmers generally, by nature, are optimists. If they have a bad year as a result of the weather, they always say that the next year will be better, and they are always hoping. Governments successively have taken farmers for granted because they know
farmers like the rural way of life, enjoy their work, hard as it is, with long hours, and, nonetheless, still prefer it to working in a factory, running a business in a city, being a professional or living in a large metropolis. Successive governments have assumed that no matter how bad conditions were on the back concession, the people would stay. You cannot live on love. You cannot live in the past. You cannot remain a farmer simply because you like the fresh air on the back concession. We have reached the point where it is financially impossible for a growing number of farmers to remain on the farm. The banks are either foreclosing or putting such pressure on the farmers as to make their lives miserable. Many are going bankrupt.
Ontario, for example, has been hard hit. Last year in the province of Ontario there were 27 farmers who went out of business. That may not sound like a lot when looking at the total number, but 27 farms going belly-up represents millions of dollars. More than that, it represents back-breaking years of hard work and sweat, all for a dream, an ideal; not a rich life but a comfortable one. Those hopes and dreams are down the tube, not because the farmers were lazy or inefficient, it is not because there is not a market out there. It is because the government has deliberately, through the Governor of the Bank of Canada, set interest rates at such a high level they cannot borrow. There are no further extensions on their line of credit and their cash flow is drying up. This is indeed a very serious matter.
Farm incomes in 1982 are projected to decline by 21 per cent over 1981. Interest charges have tripled since 1977. In 1981, farmers paid out more in interest charges than their projected income for 1982. Credit is now almost as big an item of overhead as feed. The feed goes for a useful purpose. The credit goes for two-legged hogs-the bankers.
My party does not see this bill as something to pin our hopes on. The private money market is very high at present. The minister has not brought in any changes to the Bank Act or Income Tax Act that would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to offer a tax break to people investing in FCC/agri-bonds. However, I would urge him to press the cabinet for such a change because agriculture desperately needs more low-cost credit.
This government doled out a paltry $45 million in low-interest loans through the Farm Credit Corporation. Part of this bill is to authorize those loans. It was a good idea, but much more money is needed if we are to rescue the many deserving young farmers who invested money in good faith and now see those investments going down the drain. We need these farmers desperately. The workers in my riding who produce farm machinery need these farmers. The many hungry people around the world need these farmers.
It has always bothered me when we discuss major farm problems that one third of the world population goes to bed hungry. Indeed, one third of the world population is starving.
March 30, 1982

This country has fantastic resources. Farming is certainly one of them. We have the expertise, the know-how and the land. We know how to look after that land and make it produce. We have a farm force in this country second to none in the world in intelligence, integrity, education, skills, know-how and determination. We can manufacture all the farm implements we need right here, yet last year we had a net imbalance in agricultural products to the tune of $1.34 billion. That is another mess which the Liberal government has thrown at us.
We have a small population. We can produce far more than we do. We could export far more. We could even give away a great deal of our farm produce if the government paid the farmers a decent price for their investment, hard work and expertise.
What is the government doing? It is doing everything it can to dissuade young people from farming. The government is doing everything it can to depress not only economically, but emotionally those farmers who are struggling to keep their heads above water. Through its high interest rate policy, the government is doing everything it can to make farming almost an impossibility.
What young person today 18 or 19 years of age who was born on a farm would think of buying out his father for half a million or a million dollars when he knows he can work his whole lifetime and never own that property, unlike his father and grandfather who had that sense of accomplishment after years of hard work? Then we have the problem of farmers who at the end of their working life, because of the changes in the budget with respect to the IAACs, are not able to retire as comfortably as they would like.
Farmers do not want charity. They do not want any special treatment. What they want from this government is some consideration for the very severe economic squeeze in which they now find themselves. They are asking for decent prices and interest rates. In fact, the entire country is in trouble as a result of the high interest rate policy which is driving farmers off the land.
At the present time, beef and pork producers are in the most trouble with cash crop farmers not far behind. We have heard a lot of talk from the minister about having a new hog stabilization plan in place by April 1. What do we see? We see nothing, and April 1 is just 48 hours away.
We have heard a lot of talk from the minister about a new plan for beef producers and maybe a new marketing board system. What are the results so far-nothing. We are watching an entire industry in deep trouble and here we are debating a bill that will help just a little when a lot of help is required. The over-all interest rate policy of the government must be changed, but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) must do more to provide the tools to agriculture so that farmers can help themselves.
I would like to quote a few more statistics. Let us look at the return on labour, management and equity as a percentage of equity. We have to look at farms today as a small business or industry. In 1971, the percentage was 6.5 per cent. It rose to an all-time high of 10.9 per cent in 1974. In 1980 it had fallen
Farm Loans
to 4 per cent. This is one of the few, if not the major industry in this country that is going down successively year by year. It is not even holding its own.
Let us look at realized net income as a percentage of total cash receipts. In 1971 it was 28 per cent. In 1974 it rose to 40 per cent. In 1981 it was down to 22 per cent, and the projection for 1982 is 18 per cent. We can see that the battle farmers are fighting is downhill all the way.
Is it any wonder that many are voluntarily giving up farming? Is it any wonder that there are more and more bankruptcies every year? Is it any wonder that farmers' young sons and daughters do not want anything to do with farming? They would rather go to the city where hopefully they can find steady jobs. What will happen to our rural way of life? Just because the banks, thanks to this government, want to gouge farmers and take the last pound of flesh and the last drop of blood from them, will we lose a whole way of life? Will we lose half of those 250,000 farmers?
I started my speech by saying that when I moved to Brant county in southern Ontario in 1959, there were 2,300 farmers. That is not bush country. That is some of the finest farming country in Canada. Today there are 800 farmers. How much longer will this continue? Will it continue until there are only 100,000 farmers in the entire country. What is the bottom line of Governor Bouey and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen)? Is the bottom line a thousand farm bankruptcies a year- two thousand? What is the bottom line when it comes to broken dreams and lost hope? Those are the questions the governor of the Bank of Canada, in his so-called valiant effort to fight inflation, should keep in mind.
Many economists love to juggle figures, percentages and decimal points, but every time we look at these figures we should remember that they represent human beings, most of whom are part of a long tradition of a rural way of life and farming. They are proud to be farmers. They are proud to be producing products the country and the world desperately need, yet they are being kicked around on almost every side. They are being kicked around by banks, the Farm Credit Corporation itself, the government and the Bank of Canada. I do not know how much longer they can take it.
I have sent several appeals to the Minister of Agriculture from farmers in my riding who are financially on their last legs. Most of them were turned down at the agency level of the Farm Credit Corporation. One or two got as far as the appeal board. I appealed to the minister on their behalf, and to the best of my knowledge tonight not one of them was given a break. The old argument was that the FCC cannot be overruled and that the appeal board cannot be overruled. These are not fly-by-night farmers, they are well-established farmers who are lacking in only one thing. They are not lacking in determination, ambition or desire to work, but in cash flow. Surely to God the Minister of Agriculture can come up with something better than another $45 million in loans and an

interest rate of 16.75 per cent, which is three times what it was five years ago.
I have spoken about farmers in my own county, but in so doing I hope it will be understood that I have spoken on behalf of farmers across Canada who find themselves in dire straits. I sincerely hope the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance, the cabinet and the Governor of the Bank of Canada will finally concede that their tight monetary policy which they first introduced in 1975 is not working in this country. I do not care about the United States, I do not care about England-it is not working here.
One of the main reasons it is not working here-and this relates to this bill and the farm industry-is that we have such a tremendous outflow of money as a result of our net deficit in trade in manufactured goods. It was $21 billion in 1980. If it were not for our raw materials and our farm exports, the overall net imbalance or deficit in trade would be horrendous. Why are we punishing primary producers who sell wheat around the world to help with our balance of payments? Why are we penalizing them? Why are we hurting them? Why are we making it almost impossible for them to go on or even to keep their heads above water? This is one of the most crucial sectors in our entire economy.
It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture has lost his clout in the cabinet. About a year ago he had many brave words to say to farm groups about the banks. He said he would do what he could. He said he would tell the bankers to smarten up and to put some heart into their transactions. I do not think he has done much. If he has tried, I do not think he has succeeded. Otherwise, why would he bring in a piece of legislation in which he demands 16.75 per cent on these government-guaranteed FCC loans?
There is something else that makes me angry. The banks are damned careful about lending other people's money. That is really what it amounts to. Every cent they lend through the FCC to a farmer is guaranteed by the government. The banks will not lose. Mr. Speaker, you know and I know that the banks never lose, but in this case many farmers will. They will lose their livelihood, unless the Minister of Agriculture improves upon Bill C-88.
I hope in the next year or so I will not have to stand here and tell this House that the number of farmers in Brant country has shrunk from 800 to only 600. I do not know what will happen to the farm economy, the rural way of life and the farm industry itself if we do not get things turned around, if we do not put a little humanity back into our planning and our legislation and if we do not let farmers get on with the job they like most. They do not do it just to make money, but they want to keep their heads above water. They want to work and produce and have a reasonable return on their investment and hard work.
