Mr. Speaker, normally I am able to say it is a pleasure to rise and speak about a bill, but such is not the case tonight. We are at the third reading stage of this bill. It was given first reading and we had a full debate at second reading on the principle of the
bill. Hon. members on this side of the House and, indeed, some government backbenchers, speaking about the principle of the bill generally, agreed that farmers need more assistance. Hon. members on all sides of the House then suggested in committee a large number of improvements to the bill in an effort to demonstrate that bills emanating from this House genuinely reflect the work, skills, efforts and knowledge of individual members. Unfortunately, those ideas were not accepted by the government and the minister responsible, and now we find that the bill is back in its original form, as it came to us from the bureaucracy through the cabinet. To my mind that is regrettable because this has often been the case. This indicates to me that this Parliament is not playing the role it should. Our collective wisdom should be brought to bear on problems or situations in such a way as to improve our country.
Perhaps you were in the chair this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, when an amendment from this side was rejected. It was a perfectly sound and logical amendment which would have improved the bill and the condition of farmers in this country, yet it was rejected. I really wonder why it has to be that way. Why is it that a government in power does not accept good amendments or suggestions from members of the House of whatever party? I believe hon. members in the back benches opposite have to take more individual responsibility for representing the genuine interest of their constituencies.
I doubt that this FCC bill even qualifies as a band-aid measure because the amounts of money involved are so small. The FCC has done a lot of good things for the farmers of this country and could do much more if it had the financial wherewithal; and it could have the financial wherewithal, Mr. Speaker.
Government expenses this year will increase by 22 per cent but its revenue sources have also increased enormously. Revenues from oil are coming in by the trainload and buildings to store the money cannot be put up fast enough. The government is taking all the new sources of sales tax but nothing is available for the farm community. Being of a socialist turn of mind the government wants to get into all sorts of new ventures rather than keeping the existing areas strong. This can be seen in the estimates as they relate to established programs financing, health care and post-secondary education. The blue book shows a cut of some $469 million in these areas. After the government had expanded into these programs and got the provinces involved it decided to pull out, leaving the burden on the provinces. Some of them cannot pick up the difference, Mr. Speaker. Seven provinces east of Sasksatchewan have enormous deficits and for the federal government to unload this extra burden on them is unfair.
When you contrast the band-aid measure this bill offers with the incredible harm the government has wreaked on the farm community with its budget measures, its energy security bill, the economic policy including high interest rates and deficits, you will see just how shameful it is, Mr. Speaker. If I
March 30, 1982

were a government backbencher I would be ashamed to go into my riding and tell people that this is what we are doing for farmers. The farmers I represent would not tolerate it, Mr. Speaker. They would probably beat me up and kick me out of the riding and, quite properly so. That does not seem to happen to government backbenchers. They seem to be able to go into their ridings and get away with this. That is just amazing, because it is clear that they are not representing their constituents' interests.
I believe we should always start out with the thought of what Canada would be and remember what Canada was in 1968. We were a unified nation then, with Expo 67 just behind us. We had an incredible sense of what it was to be Canadian. We had a new, fresh Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and a new, fresh government. People were expecting great things. We had balanced budgets and the national debt was almost non-existent. We had a first rate health insurance plan, a medicare plan and post-secondary education. Because of low tuition fees tens of thousands of students from modest-income families had the benefit of university education and were able to go out and develop exciting careers for themselves. Farmers were healthy and wealthy; they were prosperous. As a nation we were growing. There was a sense that the country was charging ahead and starting to fulfil its real role in the world as a peace-keeper and supplier of food.
Where are we today? There is a separatist government in the province of Quebec. There is incredible disunity between Anglophone Canadians and Francophone Canadians. There is incredible disunity between rural Canadians and urban Canadians. The first separatist member has been elected to a legislature in the west. We have a national deficit of over $14 billion per year and the accumulated national deficit is over $100 billion. The cost of interest to service that debt amounts to some $17 billion. That $17 billion is not spread evenly over the population, Mr. Speaker, but is concentrated in the hands of people with wealth. This means we are developing a class society.
If you had possessed $1 million at the beginning of the year what would you have done with it, Mr. Speaker? Would you have put it in a business to develop jobs and a future for young people? Of course not, because the risks are just enormous. You would have loaned it to your government at 19.5 per cent interest and at the end of the year you would have had $195,000 in your pocket, having taken no risk at all.
This government is creating a class society of very, very rich and very, very poor. That is exactly what is happening in many Third World countries today as a result of totalitarian government where there is a concentration of power in a monarch, a dictator or, in a socialist nation, where all decisions are made by a small group of men and women in a cabinet and in a bureaucracy. No country that has permitted power to be concentrated in a small group has been successful.
The only way to success is when the capital of a nation is divided into millions and millions of decisions-farmers making decisions with respect to their small amount of capital, for instance. An hon. member who spoke earlier told us that at
Farm Loans
one time there had been 2,300 farmers in his riding and that now there are only 800. That was 2,300 people making decisions on their portion of the national income, Mr. Speaker.
What is happening at the federal level. There are now over 400 Crown corporations, and all of them have special taxing provisions and therefore are not carrying their fair share of the tax load. The tax base is being eroded and as a result the rest of us pay more taxes but we do not have a proportionate say in the decisions made about the income of this nation. That is being drained into the central government where 36 men and women in the cabinet and a bureaucracy make the decision about how our wealth should be spent.
The hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) has often said that we all know what a slave is; it is simply someone whose human rights have been taken away completely and all decisions with respect to that person are made by the master. The slave in an economic sense is someone who is taxed 100 per cent and all the economic rent from that person and all the decisions respecting that rent are made by other people.
In this nation, when we add up the taxes paid to all levels of government, we find that 55 per cent of our individual economic rent goes to government. That means that somebody else makes the decisions about how it is spent, so we are 55 per cent slaves. And as the hon. member asks, how long do we permit this to go on-until we are 70 per cent, 80 per cent, or 100 per cent slaves, as is the case in so many other nations? We have to draw the line, Mr. Speaker. I believe that if the backbenchers opposite were to reflect the true interests of their constituents they would put a stop to this.
I have pointed out that in 1968 when the Liberal government came to power there was a tremendous feeling of national unity in the country and we were all climbing the mountain, so to speak, as a nation. As a result of $469 million coming out of the estimates for the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan), concerning post-secondary education, and for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), concerning our health system, these programs are now in disarray. Farmers are dropping like flies. The government has dissipated the trust that people put in it when it was First elected, and it has been elected continuously but it has not been honouring that trust. The Prime Minister has an obligation to think of all regions of the country and to make a genuine effort to ensure that they feel comfortable in the nation. He has failed in that fundamental trust, that fiduciary relationship.
Mackenzie King understood that and had members in all regions of the country. He had powerful members and ministers in every region. Prime Minister St. Laurent and Prime Minister Diefenbaker would never have done to the nation what this Prime Minister has done. As a result we have an elected separatist government in Quebec and an elected separatist member in the west. We also have an incredible alienation which saddens me as a Canadian. No longer are we charging up the mountain to conquer the world and be a powerful nation in support of peace, security and decency in the world. We cannot represent that to the world because we

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
are not unified within ourselves. This goes back to the man at the top and the men and women around him.
Back in 1974-76 the government felt it could make decisions with a small cabinet and bureaucracy rather than take advantage of millions and millions of individual decisions. At that time there was a surplus of grain which could not be sold, and we were at the peak of our beef production cycle. What did the government do in its wisdom? It collected statistics and had people sitting at desks in Ottawa making decisions. Rather than trusting farmers, it establised the LIFT program and threw open the borders to the importation of more beef, with the result that we were swamped with beef. It destroyed the cattle market. We paid farmers to sow their land into pasture. As a result there was a dramatic increase in beef production and the bottom fell out of the beef market. We lost thousands and thousands of beef men in the country. At the same time grain had suddenly disappeared.
Had there been proper marketing there would not have been a grain surplus, and there was a crying need for food in the world. The previous speaker gave statistics as to the number of people who go to bed hungry every night. We should never cut back production in the farm community. We should be doing everything possible to enhance more production. I wanted to give another example of government believing it could do better, and I have more examples which I will give later. Every farmer who voted for the Liberal Party in 1980 has been betrayed; they have been genuinely stabbed in the back.
I should like now to deal with capital gains tax. Canada was developed by poor people who came from other lands because there was no chance in the social or economic structures of their countries to get ahead. This started in the early 1600s with French Canadian farmers along the St. Lawrence as well as those who settled in Nova Scotia. Then there were the United Empire Loyalists after the American war of independence. Next we developed the west. Millions of our ancestors came from every country in the world to obtain land. They knew that if they obtained a piece of this territory they could make decisions for themselves. They were prepared to work hard, to live and to die young, because it was tough on the western plains. As a result, we have all had a chance and are surely better off for it.
Not once was there a tax upon the capital of those farms. It was believed then that people had a right to work hard, to amass a bit of capital and to make decisions. Millions of those decisions led to a wise over-all result. The situation was different than it was in the socialist and totalitarian states from where they came where all decision-making on the capital and wealth of the nation was in the hands of a small group.
I recall a debate in the House some time ago when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) indicated that his family was on the same parcel of land in the province of Quebec for nine generations. That will never happen again. The Lalonde family will not be on that land nine generations from now. It will probably be there for one more generation, or perhaps two at the most. The capital gains tax is such that the land cannot be passed on to the next generation
which usually has only one member who wants to be a farmer. The other members of the family usually leave the farm to become doctors, lawyers or teachers. Because of the enormous increase in the value of land due to inflation, land cannot be transferred to a member of the next generation. Farmers cannot do justice to the other members of the family because values have risen so much that they do not have adequate cash to leave land to one member of the family and cash to the others. It is impossible for the person taking over the farm to assume an equal burden and pay off the other sons and daughters. This has virtually become impossible, with the result that farmers are leaving.
As the last speaker indicated, farmers in his area have dropped from 2,300 to 800. Some of them were sold to existing farmers, often corporations. They will continue to concentrate and become bigger and bigger. Then we will find big industry becoming involved in farm production, which will want a rate of return of 20 per cent, like the oil industry. Canadians will be worse off and paying through the nose. Indeed, I expect Canadians will be lined up for food, as is the case in Poland, before they realize it.
It is a shame that the government never directs its attention to the fact that we are an enormous food importer. Despite the fact that we have a small population, some of the best farm land in the entire world, and a skilled and dedicated farming community which is determined to make the country work, we are enormous importers of food. We are not self-sufficient in many items but we could be; it is a shame.
The role of government has increased enormously. In the energy area we see a government which believes it can operate the entire oil industry with Crown corporations, it is in for the lesson of its life. Regretfully the people who pay for those lessons are the taxpayers of the nation. We poured $2 billion into Petro-Canada for the government to have a "window" on the oil industry. Now that it has a window on the oil industry, is the industry any better for it? Is there more oil in the country? Is the price of gasoline at the pump any cheaper? It is not one cent cheaper, and it will not be.
Before the government became involved, the oil industry was the most regulated industry in the country. The provinces decided whether leases would be granted and where. The provinces decided all environmental considerations and the costs. The provinces decided the rate of production from the well based upon conservation measures. The federal government decided the price of the oil and whether any would be exported. When governments control where they drill, how fast they produce, the price, and whether it is exported, what is the oil industry? It is a utility.
We were really paying multinational corporations a fee for the cost of their money. They had the front-end load to buy leases from the provinces, to pay the Canadian service industry, to conduct seismic studies, to drill wells, to do the mud-ding, the cementing, the steelwork and the production, to build pipelines, to do the refining, to build further pipelines and to pay truckers and retailers. All this part of the industry was
March 30, 1982

Canadian-owned. We were just getting the capital to develop from multinationals, and the cost of the capital was between 3 per cent and 5 per cent.
The government came along, believing it needed a window on the industry, and converted equity, which was costing 3 per cent to 5 per cent, to debt. We borrowed $2 billion from people with money, and we are paying 19.5 per cent interest on it. We bought shares. We had to borrow that money in other countries, therefore the flow of money out of Canada today is 19.5 per cent as compared with 3 per cent to 5 per cent for equity.
This is totally absurd because we went through this during the 1920s and 1930s. The bulk of the capital in this country was then in the form of debt. Most of it came from Britain. In those bad years capital flowed out of the country because of the interest rate. All the bright intellectuals, the Liberal reformers, the CCFers at that time and the intellectuals who were speaking from the universities, all said, we have to stop that. We have to convert it to equity because then the flow of money out of the country will be in the form of dividends. If there is a good year, there is a dividend. If there is a bad year, no money leaves the country. The great debate occurred and the solution was to change that debt to equity which is precisely what happened. But this government comes along and reverses the policy, and it is costing Canadians very dearly.
No doubt you read a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, that some $10 billion has flowed out of this country as a result of the National Energy Program. This has dramatically affected our farmers, as 1 will point out to you in a moment. That money did not produce any new wells. It was used to buy back equity in the form of shares. Statistics Canada reported that an additional $8 billion has moved out of Canada. The government knows the money has gone but it does not know where it has gone. I can tell you where that money has gone. It came from the pockets of our own citizens, modest income citizens and our Canadian businesses, particularly those in the oil and gas industry and it has been invested in the United States.
If you visit Denver today, it is just like Calgary was before the National Energy Program came into being. In Denver there is a dynamic climate of expansion with people investing money to find oil. Some lose a lot, but they find a little. But they are finding almost enough now to make the United States oil self-sufficient.
At one time the United States was importing over eight million barrels of oil a day. Now the United States imports only four million barrels of oil a day. The United States will become oil self-sufficient. The irony of that is, the United States is achieving that goal with our money. In the meantime, Canada still imports 450,000 barrels of oil a day. The goal of self-sufficiency has been lost.
Some of our western oil wells are being shut down because the government has made a decision to continue importing oil. All that money, $3 billion or $4 billion a year, creates jobs in Saudi Arabia, Mexico, Nigeria and Venezuela. This defies
Farm Loans
rational understanding, and it makes me wonder what is going on over on the government side.
People are taking money out of Canada because of the business climate here. Our ancestors came here to get a chunk of capital, a chance to build a future for themselves, their children and their grandchildren. As a result of the government nationalizing everything, concentrating decision-making power in the cabinet and a small bureaucracy, people are losing confidence, which they should. People are taking their money elsewhere. These are the same people who built this country. They now feel jeopardized living here. I can give you the names and addresses and introduce you to several leading farmers and ranchers in my riding, Mr. Speaker. They have come to me in all honesty and sincerity. Already three or four of them have sold their Canadian assets, taken the money and moved to the United States.
The Liberal government is doing to this country what previous politicians have done to countries around the world, forcing their citizens to uproot themselves, go to a strange land where a strange language is spoken. Yet people who came here were prepared to endure that pain for a generation so their children, their grandchildren and their great-grandchildren would have the opportunity to succeed. People are leaving Canada now because of the uncertainty.
I have talked to many farmers about the Farm Credit Corporation bill and the budget. Farmers know what the problem is. We learned the lesson in the west in the last generation. It is a shame that we have to repeat it. The existing government is made up mostly of academics who have never met a payroll in their lives, have never operated a farm, and have no idea what it is like to produce something new. You can almost guess their past when you see them. They have been to the finest schools, the finest universities, often ending up at the London School of Economics. In the end they came out totally imbued with the idea that a small group of people can make decisions affecting this huge country of ours.
The government decided to get into deficit financing. This government took over at a time when there was a very low national debt. The budgets were balanced yearly. It decided it could offer people all sorts of programs with a low capital tax and borrow the difference. The first year everything was great. We went from 1969 right through to 1978. This government was able to buy people with their own money. But the interest to service the debt was rising. Members on this side were sounding the alarm, saying, look, folks, it cannot go on. We have been through this. But the government was able to buy people with their own money. The government got away with it.
But now the government must stop. Even the socialist Liberal government recognizes it has to stop. We are now seeing socialist taxes to match socialist programs. But what happened in the meantime? People had borrowed money for house mortgages, perhaps for houses which were too big. When we had all the programs and low tax, people had extra money. People paid too much for land, too much for businesses and too much for their homes. When there are deficits too

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
much money chases too few goods, driving up the value of those goods. We call it inflation. The situation has to stop. It is to be stopped with high interest rates.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada said, as he has warned for years, "If you, the government, will not exercise fiscal responsibility, I will exercise my duty as the Governor of the Bank of Canada and I will put up the rates. That will hurt people. It will cause unemployment." The real fault does not lie with the Governor of the Bank of Canada, it lies at the feet of this government. During all of those years it got people to believe in deficit government financing. The government did not heed the calls from this side or the calls from responsible economists. Canadians are now having to pay for it. They are dropping like flies, particularly in the farming community.
Farmers cannot tolerate high interest rates. They have a front-end load. Farmers have to borrow money in the spring to buy seed, fertilizer and enormous quantities of fuel to get the crops seeded. They have to summerfallow. They have to spray chemicals to kill weeds. They have to spray to control pests. Then in the fall they harvest the crops. Farmers have an enormous front-end load, and high interest rates simply destroy them.
Other societies have learned this fact. The admonition in the Bible about usurious interest rates is not in the Bible because of some religious doctrine, it is there as a result of a society's practical experience, having endured high interest rates. It failed because of high interest rates. That is what is happening to Canada today. High interest rates so demoralize people that they drop like flies and then society turns to all sorts of radical political solutions. This happened in the west in earlier generations. That is why we had the Social Credit Party and the United Farmers' Party. The CCF grew out of those economic dislocations of governments taking people into deficit financing.
Farmers have the extra burden of high energy costs, for which this bill does nothing. When our government was in power there was a special tax credit for farmers to help them with their high energy costs. Farmers are enormous consumers of energy. The present Liberal government threw out that rebate. Instead, it imposed a series of taxes. I saw the figures for the province of Alberta. A litre of gasoline in Alberta is 33 cents. There are six individual taxes imposed by the federal government on that litre of gasoline. The Alberta government has one charge, the ownership royalty, which goes to the citizens as owners. When you get to the bottom of these figures you find the federal government collects 42 per cent of the value of that 33-cent litre. Just think about the fact that 42 per cent of the value goes to the federal government through six taxes. Twenty per cent of the value of a litre of gasoline goes to the people of Alberta as owners and the remaining percentage value goes to the industry for producing, refining and selling the gasoline to us.
The farmers bear a triple load. They not only pay on the fuel they use in their cars, but they have to buy chemicals, fertilizer and extra quantities of fuel to produce food. Why, as a wise
Parliament, should we not give them special rebates? If we on this side formed the government we would, because the Progressive Conservative Party understand the special plight of farmers. Unfortunately, the Liberal government does not.
Another thing happening is that high inflation is leading us into a situation where we will soon become a society of landlords and serfs. According to statistics, the number of owner farmers is dropping dramatically while the number of tenant farmers is increasing. That is a quantum leap backwards some 900 years in history, Mr. Speaker, to feudal times. The government ridiculed Khomeini for taking Iran back some 1,300 years in terms of religious doctrine. This government is taking Canada back 900 years to feudal times. Serfs have no security of tenancy, so someone who wants to be a farmer has no guarantee that his children or grandchildren can be farmers. That is exactly what kings did in feudal times. They would give a farm to a man because he was a good soldier and had served the monarch well, but at the end of his life the land came back to the king and he gave it to someone else. That is exactly what is going to happen in Canada as a result of these deficits which are leading us to a class society.
The cheap food policy, Mr. Speaker, which even Liberal members now admit we have, was a concious policy of this government. In 1968 we were charging up the mountain, we were excited about being Canadians, we were unified and our governments were pulling together in a co-operative form of federalism. Canadians were enjoying a rising level of wealth, they had more cash in their pockets, and this was a great opportunity for the government to oversee a distribution of wealth to the farmer in order to sustain their farms and permit the same number of farmers to continue. Canadians spend some 17 per cent of their income on food, and this cheap food policy has been borne primarily by the farmer.
Seventy-five years ago, when the land was first broken, the soil was almost 100 per cent fertile. Now, a relatively short time later, we are down to nearly 50 per cent. At the present rate of decline the soil will be sterile in another 50 years time, and that is a perfect recipe for another dust bowl.
The Roman empire fell because it did not look after its agriculture. There were other reasons, such as getting into deficits and the concentration of power. What is now the Sahara desert in Northern Africa was once the world's most fertile area. Government's throughout the Middle East had enormously productive land. The Cedars of Lebanon were destroyed by governments which did not pay attention to their farmers, their forests and their land. Members opposite may think we will not one day have food lines, and I hope we do not, but, I believe, at the rate of progression of these things we will.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should not be going across this land bragging that Canadians pay less for a basket of food than people in any other country in the world. He should be going into the cities and explaining to people why we need to spend more than 17 per cent of our income on food. It probably should be in the order of 23 per cent to 25 per cent
March 30, 1982

so that farmers can remain on the land and improve productivity. Only then will we have a future for our children and grandchildren. I just do not understand why members opposite do not have this feeling for the future that we certainly have on this side. They should adopt the tradition of the Iroquois nation which required band leaders, before making any decision, to think about the effect of those decisions seven generations later. As a result of that policy the Iroquois survived for many generations until we came along with our guns and alcohol.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, where are the members opposite when we speak of capital gains? They seem to be in favour of them. Where are they with respect to energy costs? They rejected an energy rebate for farmers, and, indeed, have added six separate taxes which increases the cost of production enormously. They do not speak out against deficits, therefore we can assume they are in favour of them. They must also be in favour of the inflation which flows out of deficits, and they must be in favour of high interest rates which ultimately flow from inflation.
Mr. Speaker, there is no need for all of this. Let us never forget what Canada was like in 1968. Government's can and do hurt people, Mr. Speaker, and the Liberal Party is a prime example of that. The government will be cited in the textbooks of future generations as a classic example of how a socialist party, trying to concentrate wealth, can take the energetic and dynamic young people climbing a mountain and destroy them.

subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we near the end of this debate I would like to spend a few minutes recapping the arguments made in this discussion. First of all, the main thrust of the amendment is to increase the amount of capital which the Farm Credit Corporation has available to lend to farmers. The amendments will mean that the FCC is no longer restricted to the government as a source of funds. Possible sources of funds will be retiring farmers who have managed during good years to accumulate a bit of a surplus. We are also told that sources such as pension funds, foreign and domestic banks, and government bonds will also be available to the FCC. However, none of this is spelled out in the act and the minister was not very specific in committee as to just which source of funds the FCC would first be turning to.
It has been assumed, Mr. Speaker, that there would be some form of agribond or small business bond, call it what you will, the form of which would require changes in the Income Tax Act, and a definite policy from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Those changes have not been forthcoming. There has been no indication by the Minister that such changes will be made available so that these sources of funds can be utilized by the FCC.
I believe hon. members on all sides of this chamber have in mind a system of taxation which would defer tax on capital gains on the sale of farm properties, as long as the owner of the funds reinvested the money in an acceptable way so the money could be borrowed again by farmers who are continuing on in
Farm Loans
business. This would allow the Farm Credit Corporation or the credit unions out in the country to have access to this money. They would not have to pay the normal rate of interest because payment had not been made on the capital gains. Therefore, it is usually estimated that a compensatory rate would be approximately half of the current interest rate. The lending institution, whether the Farm Credit Corporation or the credit union, could relend that money to beginning or expanding farmers for about one per cent more than that. This would certainly maintain the refinancing of agriculture from one generation to the other at lower rates. This fits in with our concept in this party of attempting to make sectors of the economy more or less self-sufficient in terms of refinancing to ensure growth of that industry in future years.
There has also been some discussion during this debate about the farm income problem. Our party believes this is the main reason we have a shortage of farm credit. Our analysis is that the farm market prices have not been adequate. The government has not provided adequate marketing legislation and accompanying stabilization programs which would make it possible for farmers to recover their costs and a return on the efforts that they have put into their agricultural production. Because that has not occurred, farmers in this country have incurred an increasingly larger debt. We have outlined the magnitude of that debt, running from about $6 billion in 1974 to close to $22 billion at the present time. This debt has been incurred in the space of a mere eight years. Farmers are facing an annual shortfall of between $2 billion and $3 billion just to cover most of their costs. We have pointed out how the returns to agriculture have dropped to the point at which they are now approaching zero.
We have heard representations from various farm groups producing any number of commodities. They have told us a number of things about their particular sectors of agriculture. For instance, I note that grain producers in western Canada are now at the point at which most of them are no longer able to carry out continuous cropping. For those hon. members who have some doubt about my words, I would ask them to consult the latest issue of Grainews. An article by a producer of grain points out that for the size of farm he is operating, which is slightly larger than average, a very efficient-sized operation, the price of wheat at the farm must exceed $4.80 per bushel to enable him to continue buying the fertilizer and chemicals required to continuously crop his product. Instead, along with virtually 80 per cent of the grain farmers in western Canada, he will be taking another option starting this year. For some it will be the continuation of an option started years ago. He will be going back to a 50-50 summer fallow cropping practice.
For some hon. members who are not familiar with the prairies, let me say that about half the prairies do have enough rainfall to allow more concentrated cropping production. However, with the current price of wheat and barley, the most profitable option now is go back to a 50-50 summer fallow practice. Total production will be down, but the financial position on each of those farms will be better by switching back to that old practice.

March 30, 1982
Farm Loans
We spoke to farmers from Ontario, some from Bruce and Grey counties. I understand that the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) will be speaking soon. I spoke to corn producers from eastern Ontario as well. They told us that even if they got their land for nothing, given the current cost of seeding and caring for an acre of corn, and given the current cost of fertilizer, chemicals, fuel and machinery, the return on that acre of corn will not pay its own way. We know that the same situation exists in the livestock industry. We hear many jokes around the auction markets. Farmers ask each other how things are going, and one will tell the other that things are going a little better this year as he will produce only 50 per cent or 25 per cent as many cattle as he did last year. Their objective is to lose less money.
I think, being realistic, we must recognize that this bill, granting a bit more capital to the Farm Credit Corporation, will do very little to solve the real problem in agriculture today. Another $45 million or $75 million is a drop in the bucket considering the $2 billion to $3 billion in losses that the farmers will have to put up with this year.
The government is not willing to infuse money into agriculture. It has not provided improvements to the marketing system, and it has not provided stabilization programs. We are one day away from a deadline imposed by the minister himself for a stabilization program for hogs. We will await with interest the coming of April 1. The amount of activity that has gone on between the provinces and the farm groups would indicate that the minister has not come up with an agreement on a stabilization program for hogs. There has been no talk of improved marketing and no serious talk of improved beef marketing. As a result, farmers are going out of business.
I recently attended the annual meeting of one of the major marketing boards. It was attended by the leaders of that industry, an industry which operates under a supply management system and a cost-of-production formula. A great many delegates are not too far from bankruptcy themselves, even with the cost-of-production formula. Of course, part of the reason is that the cost-of-production formula assumes that a good chunk of the money invested in those operations can be borrowed at a rate of 11 per cent. Of course, we cannot get money at 11 per cent interest. The difference between the interest rate of 18 per cent to 21 per cent, which money really costs, and the assumed rate of 11 per cent has created a deficit in most of these operations because they relied on the assumed rate.
We have heard about bankruptcies in this debate. However, for every bankruptcy there are probably five or six farmers who are voluntarily going out of business. In this country we know that for every farmer who goes out of business, three other workers in the economy lose jobs because the economy will no longer continue to support those jobs. At the moment, well in excess of one million workers are unemployed in this country. The fiscal and monetary policy of the government has been creating a lack of jobs for workers. It has been creating unemployment for workers and farmers. When a country has unemployment it does not have production.
I have outlined some of the things that those farmers who are still in existence will do to stay in business. They will cut back grain production. Lifestock producers are also going to cut back production because of bankruptcies and market conditions. Employers in other sectors are laying people off. We have this great country gradually winding down, producing less and less, and all of this, according to the Minister of Finance and the government, to fight inflation.
How can you fight inflation by reducing the amount of goods and services produced? The old economic axiom for inflation was too much money chasing too few goods, yet we are attempting to fight inflation by producing even fewer goods. It is a wrong-headed policy, and it went wrong with our agricultural policy. That is why this particular debate on agriculture and its importance to the economy in general has been an important one.
I regret that more funds were not made available to farmers, to agriculture in general, in an attempt to turn this situation around. However, I hope that some government members will at least have received the message, and they will take it to cabinet through the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and that current policy will be reversed very soon so that this country's farmers, workers and the economy can once again go forward progressively.

speechtext:
I rise with very little time remaining, Mr. Speaker, at the end of this debate on Bill C-88. It is a discussion that may not interest many people, because there is such a small number of people directly involved in agricultural production. However, many consumers, many people in Canada should have a feeling for the importance of this type of legislation, albeit legislation that falls far short of the mark we would have hoped to achieve with the changes in this bill.
This Farm Credit Corporation legislation has been ongoing now for approximately 20 years. Originally as intended it would have provided the kind of stable, secure financing that agriculture needs if it is to continue to provide the cheap food that this country is able to produce. While many people may not relate to the Farm Credit Corporation, they can certainly relate to the price of food in their baskets each week as they go to the supermarket, and in the long run it is those people we have to be concerned about.
We see a government at this point in time whose policies over the past in dealing with inflation, with interest rates and taxation policies, have put a terrific amount of pressure on consumers as well as on agriculture. At this point in time we see the agriculture community threatened with its very survival; and this survival, from the point of view of this change to the Farm Credit Corporation legislation is still not secure.
It is not secure because the capital that we are considering for the expansion of farms across the country is not necessarily
March 30, 1982

going to be provided on the basis that is required; that is to say, if we do get more capital we cannot be confident that this kind of legislation will provide interest rates that are affordable. That is the key factor, which has been pointed out by two county federations of agriculture we met with and talked with in the last few weeks. First on the list each time was the interest rate problem.
The government that was going to "wrestle inflation to the ground" now has been wrestling for long enough. They holler at Uncle Sam or they holler at somebody else when they get into trouble. It is really not the responsibility of anyone but this Liberal government to make sure that the productive sectors of the economy, whether it is agricultural or mineral areas or forestry, are able to survive and produce jobs for the country, because of the multiplier effects of this kind of production.
The changes we have in this bill are a start. They offer a potential for new sources of revenue apart from the Consolidated Revenue Fund so that the Farm Credit Corporation can expand from the limited amount of capital it has had available for agriculture.
The interest rate to be recommended we have yet to see, but the expansion of that capital will depend very much on the ability of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to convince his cabinet colleagues, and with Treasury Board in particular, of the need to provide an additional amount. This will amount to $26 million in addition to the $14 million he is asking for now, in order to bring himself into a position where he can fulfil his promise of $1 billion in additional funding for the Farm Credit Corporation.
I doubt very much, Mr. Speaker, that most of the members opposite have an understanding of that problem. I suspect that the Minister of Agriculture knows his problem, but his influence with the cabinet and his impact has been so little lately, I would have very real concern that he will be successful in that endeavour.
As we approach the end of this debate, Mr. Speaker, the important thing I would like to add is, in addition to the difficulties that might present themselves for the resolution of these problems, there is the question of what is to be done in the short term. Even with these changes in the Farm Credit Corporation financing arrangement we still have a very real short-term problem. As mentioned before, the spring planting is going to bring this into sharper focus in the next several months, particularly if we are to allow farmers the ability to even maintain a cash flow for survival, in order that they can put their crops in the ground. We have a situation now where this ability is threatened for this large segment of the agricultural community.
We need to pay immediate attention to stabilization programs. The provinces have indicated their desire to co-operate with the federal government in stabilization programs in a number of commodity areas, particularly in beef and pork. We
Farm Loans
know, because of the number of representations we have had from the federation of agriculture nationally, and from different farm organizations, that we need a moratorium on any further bank foreclosures. We need to ensure that the Small Business Development Bond system will work effectively for agricultural producers. We know that we must have additional, significant discussions with the Minister of Agriculture federally, with a hopeful impact on the federal cabinet, so that there can be arrangements, through new legislation, the old Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, or through some new mechanism, so that some of these people, with interest mounting hour by hour, will be able to come to some better arrangements or terms with their creditors and continue in the actual farm practice.
The future we have in the agricultural community, Mr. Speaker, might reflect the future we have in all of Canada. I have real concern, and I think members from across the country have a feeling for the difficulties that we might face, if we are not able to address these difficulties effectively. We are facing the possibility of upheaval, not just in the agriculture community but in the entire social structure of the country. This is being felt most directly by agriculture; and certainly in areas where auto workers, and workers in a variety of industries are being severely impacted upon by the policy we have had in the last few years.
We have a real problem, and we are threatened with the lack of response from the government so far, and its inability to deal with these problems. We are threatened with changes in the social fabric that will threaten our future as a country. We have seen regional difficulties arise and a number of other problems. We have seen people lose interest in what the federal government is doing and in what political parties are doing. In the long run that is a very serious and very real threat that is destroying the kind of spirit, the kind of hope, the kind of future we would all love this country to enjoy. Thank you.

subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION. (B) REQUEST THAT ORDER IN COUNCIL BE RESCINDED
EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION. (B) REQUEST THAT ORDER IN COUNCIL BE RESCINDED
speechtext:
I rise with respect to a question, Mr. Speaker, I put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on March 24. It had to do with promulgation of the emergency planning order by cabinet in May, 1981.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I have been speaking out against this planning order for, I think, good and justifiable reasons. The planning order in question constitutes a very serious threat to the civil liberties of Canadians. It is one to which I have taken exception for a variety of reasons.
My question to the Prime Minister on March 24 was about the plans of the government to introduce emergencies legislation. I expressed concern at that time over the fact that the present War Measures Act, which is the only legislation we have on the books at the present time specifically dealing with emergency situations, does not embody Article 4 of the International Convenant on Civil and Political Rights.
I pointed out that the minister responsible for emergency planning, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), has publicly acknowledged that an emergency situation would override those freedoms enunciated in the Charter of Rights and the War Measures Act. It simply does not provide the comprehensive legislative foundation to meet the broad range of peacetime, international and wartime contingencies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION. (B) REQUEST THAT ORDER IN COUNCIL BE RESCINDED
speechtext: When?

subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION. (B) REQUEST THAT ORDER IN COUNCIL BE RESCINDED
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary asks when the President of the Privy Council said this. It was in a speech he delivered to the conference on emergency planning and emergency arrangements. It was a federal-provincial conference reported in the July-September 1981 Digest. I will quote him specifically. The parliamentary secretary might take note of this. He said:
First, I noted that Canadian emergencies legislation does not explicitly embody the human rights safeguards set out in Article 4 of the International Convenant on Civil and Political Rights-
Like the International Convenant, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms recognizes that most human rights are not absolute and that certain limitations on them are inevitable.
He went on to say, relating to the inadequacy of the War Measures Act with respect to peacetime emergencies, as follows:
But the events of October 1970 raised serious questions about relying on the War Measures Act for dealing with domestic and peacetime emergencies.
On March 24 I asked the Prime Minister when we might expect legislation with respect to peacetime emergencies and general emergencies legislation, and when we might expect the proposals to receive first reading. The Prime Minister neglected or refused to answer that question.
I subsequently received information, through a response to the President of the Privy Council to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments,
that there is no immediate intention of introducing any emergencies legislation. What this government has done is come in by the back door. It has circumvented Parliament by the enactment of a massive emergency planning order by order in council rather than introducing emergencies legislation so that Parliament, the elected representatives of the people, has the opportunity of assessing and analysing the powers which the government intends to give itself in an extraordinary situation. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) that further in his response to the Senate and House of Commons Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments he said that the government will use the royal prerogative if a peacetime emergency arises and Parliament is dissolved or cannot otherwise be assembled. To quote him specifically, he said:
If Parliament were dissolved, or if the pace of the crisis at hand did not allow the time to assemble Parliament, the government would be forced to act in reliance on the Crown prerogative-
What we have here is the worst of both worlds. We have the government enacting this massive planning which will allow mandarins, public servants of our country, to put into place the extraordinary powers in the hands of government ministers and of the cabinet of this country. What the President of the Privy Council tells us is that if an emergency now arises, the government will take its responsibility and move to deal with that emergency.
Having acted, as the President of the Privy Council said, extra-legally-which in simple terms means outside the law- the government would then conceivably come back to Parliament asking for indemnification for actions taken without proper legislative authority. That contravenes principles, which I thought existed in our country, of government under the rule of law. If the government has no immediate intentions of asking for enabling legislation, there will be an irresistible temptation on the part of the government at the time of any emergency to put into effect this massive-and expensive, I venture to say-planning order without any parliamentary approval whatsoever. Members of the House of Commons should have an opportunity to decide what kind of legislation we want to pass, if we should pass any at all, and whether we are prepared to deal by way of legislation with emergencies of an environmental or peacetime nature. These are very important questions.
The government acts outside Parliament to put in place a huge planning order which would have severe implications for the rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens, including a national information service put forward by the Prime Minister, a food rationing program put forward by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) with the capacity of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) to take control over all of the telecommunication facilities in our country. That is not the kind of democracy of which I can be very proud. This is not the attitude of a government which is sensitive to liberties in our country.
March 30, 1982

I ask the parliamentary secretary to tell us when the elected representatives of the people of Canada will have an opportunity to debate this matter and when we will hear the proposals of the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-QUERY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION. (B) REQUEST THAT ORDER IN COUNCIL BE RESCINDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very unfortunate that the opposition has tried to exploit this issue politically. The hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) said that the government has attempted to circumvent Parliament by giving itself a number of powers and enacting a massive planning order. What has to be understood by the Canadian public is that what the government did was bring up to date an emergency planning order which has been on the books for many, many years. I have traced the order back into the forties. It was most recently brought up to date in 1965.
The responsibility for drawing up certain plans, about which the opposition has made the most noise, is that given to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), and the hon. member knows exactly what 1 am talking about. Yesterday I read the 1965 order, and that phrase was there virtually verbatim. What I am saying to the hon. member is that that particular item was in an emergency planning order which was on the books the entire time the Clark government was in office and the hon. member was a minister. If it offended him, why did his government not rescind it? Did that government rescind it? Of course it did not rescind it. Why did that government not rescind it? The reason it did not rescind it is that obviously it is incumbent upon any responsible government to have in place certain plans to deal with emergencies which may arise. It is as simple as that.

subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-CRITERIA FOR RELEASE OF CRIMINALS
EMERGENCY MEASURES-CRITERIA FOR RELEASE OF CRIMINALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday I rose in the House to ask a question of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) about the provisions within orders in council that deal with emergency planning and the powers given to the Solicitor General to empty jails so that people who had not been convicted of a crime could be put in them and then they could be used as civilian internment camps. There are several things that disturb me about this whole issue of civilian internment camps and the so-called emergency planning orders, Mr. Speaker. What disturbs me most is the amount of deception in the ranks of government and the statements made by government members.
The first deception came when I first raised the question last October 29 in this House. At that time I put much the same kind of question to the Solicitor General. He replied, at page 12291 of Hansard, in part as follows:
Madam Speaker, there are no such orders in council.
After that subject began to be ventilated properly he naturally admitted that there are such orders in council.
The other day, when I asked him about the efficacy of releasing people convicted of a criminal offence in order to make room for people who had not been charged with a criminal offence, he said, as reported at page 15766 of Hansard:
Madam Speaker, the member can see from the question he has asked what difficult issues arise.
I think that qualifies as the greatest understatement of the year. Why bring in an order in council to deal with regulations in an emergency situation if there is no legislation in place that ought to limit those emergency powers? It seems to me that the correct approach is the customary one; bring in the legislation and then bring in the regulations.
I have heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say in the House several times in answer to questions that if there are people who are aggrieved by the process of emergency planning, if it should happen that people should be incarcerated without due process of law, as a result of the new Charter of Rights and Freedoms they will have recourse to the courts. I listened to that with interest, Mr. Speaker.
The Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) ought to be an authority on the subject. On December 17, 1980, he spoke in this House in a debate I initiated for the production of papers. At page 14183 of Hansard he said:
-I would hope that the following brief description of the anticipated procedures would help to alleviate the concerns about possible internment requirements that have been expressed by hon. members.
As he was the lead-off speaker for the government I take it he was its spokesman. I believe he spoke from a prepared text so

March 30, 1982
Adjournment Debate
we have to assume that he was speaking on behalf of the government. He listed five different procedures that will be available to the citizens of Canada if they feel they have been aggrieved by the process initiated by the emergency planning orders. At page 14183 of Hansard he said:
First, it is and will continue to be a function of the security service-
We still do not know what was involved in the security service for Canada. He continued:
Second, as a safeguard against possible abuse, any intelligence to be used in support of this identification program must first be presented for examination to a review committee composed of senior officials of the security service-
Third, the review committee would examine the information presented to ensure that stringent guidelines protecting the rights and civil liberties of individuals are respected.
Fourth, only if the Parliament of Canada declared a national emergency in relation to war or public order and subject to the passage by this House of specific enabling legislation, could internment action actually be taken.-
Fifth, as a final safeguard against potential injustice, such legislation would guarantee a detainee the right to appeal his detention to an independent advisory committee appointed by the incumbent minister of justice-
It is important to point out that in those five steps which the Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council gave in the House on December 17 there was no mention of the judicial process or appeal to the courts. It was simply an in-house system of review committees which the government will set up.
I wonder how many Japanese during World War II found the courts available to them when they aggrieved. I wonder how many of the 465 members of the Quebec society in 1970, when they were interned without questioning, without habeas corpus, had the courts available to them for appeal. The minister has never answered the question. He needs to justify before the bar of this House the wide-sweeping powers given to him which permit him to release people convicted of criminal offences in order to make room for people who have never been charged or convicted of any crime.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alain Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-CRITERIA FOR RELEASE OF CRIMINALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to a question asked on March 24, 1982, by the member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) concerning, and I quote:

-criteria to release convicted criminals in order to make room for people who have not been convicted of a crime.
Item 6 in column 1 of Part II of the schedule to order in council PC 1981-1305 of May 21, 1981, authorized the Solicitor General in the case of war to:
-facilitate the selective reduction and transfer of prison populations to provide for the establishment of civilian internment camps.
I should like to emphasize that the order makes clear that these proposed measures will only come into effect in the case of war. They are not available in the case of lesser emergencies. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has done a disservice to the cause of emergency planning by claiming falsely that the government has already established civilian
internment camps. I should also like to point out that the present order in council provides for essentially the same measures which were contained in its predecessor, PC 19651041, published in The Canada Gazette, Part II, on June 23, 1965, assigning responsibility at the time to the Minister of Justice.
The tasks relating to internment in wartime, transferred from the Minister of Justice to the Solicitor General by order in council, have been public knowledge since 1965, and the opposition has nothing more to attack now than it had at any time since 1965.

As the minister indicated, Mr. Speaker, a responsible government should be prepared to protect Canadians in a wartime emergency, and that is the reason for this order in council, namely, to provide the authority for planning such measures. There is no question of their implementation.

I should also like to note that so far this matter has a low priority. I have not yet seen any options from my officials in this regard, and none are yet in preparation. Let me assure the hon. member, however, that any options developed, including an option reflecting Item 7 in Part II of the Schedule to PC 1981-1305, would be required to include all safeguards for civil liberties provided in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and to ensure that the safety of the public would have the fullest consideration. The only regulations now in existence in this area are those which were used in World War II to incarcerate civilians. These regulations were a serious infringement of civil rights at the time and should not be the sole basis available on the shelf to turn to in the urgent event of a war crisis.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-PROVISIONS FOR SINGLE PARENT MEMBERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PAY BE INCREASED
CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-PROVISIONS FOR SINGLE PARENT MEMBERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PAY BE INCREASED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome the new Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Henderson). This is the first opportunity I have had to deal with him in his new position as parliamentary secretary. I hope he proves to be more enlightened and enlightening than his predecessor and his minister in answering questions that I have put to them in this House.
I want to expand on my question of yesterday and address what the Department of National Defence refers to as "People and People Progress".
Yesterday, I directed a question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) about the salaries of low-ranked Armed Forces personnel. What prompted me to raise that question was the sad case of Rhonda Gordon, a private at CFB Winnipeg, and a single parent. Right now a private's salary is $705 per month or an annual gross of $8,460. For comparison, the poverty line according to Statistics Canada for a family of
March 30, 1982

two in a city the size of Winnipeg is $9,912. A private like Rhonda Gordon, struggling to raise her five-year-old daughter, falls almost $1,500 below the poverty line.
From her gross salary, deductions were taken for her quarters, which she shared with another woman in order to save money, and for her rations. That left her with a take-home pay of only $360 a month, which was not enough to feed her daughter and pay for daycare, which is not provided at the base. Instead she paid her parents living in Gimli, some 60 miles from CFB Winnipeg, $120 a month to care for her daughter.
I am sure members of this House can well understand that Rhonda Gordon wanted to be with her daughter. But when she approached one of her supervisors at CFB Winnipeg, he advised her to apply for welfare as a protest over the pay received by first-year privates. She was advised to apply for welfare. What kind of life is that? Our first-year privates live below the poverty line, and are then advised to apply for social assistance.
In the fall of 1979 the base social worker at CFB Calgary reported that 400 families there were eligible for welfare. You can be sure the slick recruitment ads for the Armed Forces do not mention anything about that. When I think of it, "There's no life like it" may be the safest and most accurate promise that can be made by our Armed Forces to new recruits.
What did Rhonda Gordon do? In her own words she pulled a "Klinger." Refusing to go on welfare and to live without her daughter, she feigned mental illness and was released. It should come as no surprise that Rhonda Gordon is not the first to leave the Armed Forces because the salaries at the bottom level are too low.
When rents at CFB Calgary began their 69 per cent increase in 1979, 57 service people left the forces because they could not afford to stay. The annual attrition rate at CFB Calgary is 25 per cent. One senior officer there complained that with the rent increases which bring base housing costs into line with regional Calgary costs, his troops were now among the working poor. That was in 1979. Now two and one half years later precious little has been done to remedy the situation.
What has been the response of the Department of National Defence? In 1980 when reports of military families being eligible for social assistance benefits were made public, an Armed Forces newsletter published in Ottawa attempted to minimize the importance of the problem. It claimed stories of military families being eligible for welfare were largely based on emotion and were supported only by hypothetical examples.
Let me refer to the Calgary cases, as reported in the Montreal Gazette on May 14, 1980. Let me quote briefly from the story, leaving out the names. Mrs. A.:
-is four months pregnant. She can't afford maternity clothes, eats a lot of macaronni and cheese and has only $4 to see her family through next week.

Shortly after ... had her first baby, her husband had to take a part-time job to help pay for medical expenses.
But money problems are not the only things these women have in common. They are all married to soldiers at the Canadian Forces Base in Calgary.
Those cannot be called hypothetical, Mr. Speaker.
On November 27 the Minister took the magnanimous step of increasing armed forces salaries by 3 per cent. Even after that Rhonda Gordon is still $1500 beneath the poverty line and unable to bring her daughter to live with her.

There is nothing I can do more than that, beyond telling her that she should have known all this before she enlisted in the Armed Forces.
It is distressing, Mr. Speaker, that the minister should be so uncaring.

With respect to the particular case in question, let us examine the pay levels. On enrolment in March 1981 the pay for a private recruit was $608 monthly. On April 1, 1981, the forces were granted a pay increase of some 12.31 per cent for enlisted personnel, and then on October 1, 1981, a further adjustment of 3 per cent was made. Therefore, by anyone's calculations this would amount to an annual pay increase of just under 16 per cent-not 3 per cent as erroneously stated by the hon. member yesterday.
Thus, as of the first of October, 1981, the minimum pay that a private soldier would have received after basic training amounted to $746 per month. Then after one year of service private soldiers receive a further pay increase commonly referred to as the first level of incentive pay, which raises their earnings to $956 monthly.
By anyone's calculations these figures show that a private who enrolled in March 1981 has seen his or her salary increase
by over 55 per cent over a one-year period. I challenge the hon. member to offer other examples in the economy where an individual's salary increase over a one-year period would be so great.
If one is to subtract standard deductions for income tax, unemployment insurance, pension contributions and so on, plus accommodation-including utilities, incidentally-at $106 per month, one finds a disposable monthly income of some $543, or $271.50 every two weeks. I stress that this is disposable income, not take-home pay, as indicated by the hon. member. There is a substantial difference in the two terms and the amount is substantially more than the $180 quoted by the hon. member.
